items.title: Anthropic gets rock star welcome in public markets
items.summary: Charly Triballeau/Getty Images The AI world’s ball drop took place in Times Square yesterday, where Anthropic debuted on the Nasdaq with a 34% price pop in an IPO seen as a bellwether for the broader industry. The AI lab that former OpenAI employees founded in 2021 instantly…
items.author: Sam Klebanov
items.contentHtml:
The AI world’s ball drop took place in Times Square yesterday, where Anthropic debuted on the Nasdaq with a 34% price pop in an IPO seen as a bellwether for the broader industry.

The AI lab that former OpenAI employees founded in 2021 instantly became one of the world’s most valuable public companies:

  • ANT hit brokerages around noon, trading at $111, or 34% above the $83 price set yesterday for a pool of preferred investors. It settled at $97 by the end of the day.
  • The company’s IPO raised a record $81 billion, breaking the $75 billion record set by SpaceX in its public debut in June. Anthropic also sold $26 billion in private shares.

Though Wall Street’s willingness to snatch up Anthropic shares showed enthusiasm about the AI trade, it didn’t propel other parts of the market. The tech-heavy Nasdaq closed down 2.2%, which some analysts say was caused by investors cashing out gains from the Anthropic IPO bump and renewed anxieties about chipmakers.

More yachts are coming to San Francisco Bay: There are likely 2,800 Anthropic employees with shares now worth $10 million or more, while 600 employees are likely to have stakes valued at more than $100 million, per investment platform Hill.com. A windfall is also coming for early backers like Lightspeed Venture Partners, Iconiq, Menlo Ventures, and a VC firm co-founded by Ashton Kutcher, which owns 0.5% of Anthropic.

As for the rest of us…analysts say thatreturns from Anthropic shares will hinge on how productive the tech makes its customers, its ability to compete with rivals, and whether it can grow revenue fast enough to justify spending $900 billion on AI infrastructure. Meanwhile, Anthropic’s IPO has intensified calls from lawmakers to regulate the industry.

Anthropic has goals beyond growing your 401(k). It has legally committed to prioritizing the good of humanity by developing safe AI systems, per its Public Benefit Corporation status. Experts say this could turn off some investors, since Anthropic’s definition of public good could conflict with profits.—SK

items.title: Why everyone should be doing therapy
items.summary: I would bet my house that you’re living with something. There is some sickness, pain, or condition you’ve learned to deal with. Because there is no such thing as “perfect” health. Everyone you talk to, everyone you see on the street, everyone in the line at the coffee shop, has…
items.author: Jonny Thomson
items.contentHtml:
I would bet my house that you’re living with something. There is some sickness, pain, or condition you’ve learned to deal with. Because there is no such thing as “perfect” health. Everyone you talk to, everyone you see on the street, everyone in the line at the coffee shop, has something they have to adapt to. It might be something mild, like dry skin in the winter or being nearsighted. It might be a chronically bad back or intermittent migraines. Or, it might be something that requires more of us: diabetes tests, dialysis, the latest cancer treatment. Everyone, everywhere, is dealing with something.

Mental health is no different. I’m sometimes asked if I’m an anxious or obsessive person, and my reply is almost always the same. Yes, I can certainly feel anxious, and yes, I can display obsessive behaviors, but am I anxious or obsessive? I don’t think so. I am the way I am, and I have learned how to live with that. We all grow to deal with the world as best we can. I have strategies, tools, and ways of thinking that allow me to operate in the world, and I’m sure you do as well. The question, then, is what tools we can call upon.

The French philosopher Georges Canguilhem once argued that we shouldn’t necessarily define “health” as perfect function or as a “no boxes checked” on a health questionnaire. Instead, we should define health in terms of a “margin of tolerance” to the world’s misfortunes. To be healthy is to have hard times, experience pain, and endure mental distress, but to get back up again and to get back to living. “Health” doesn’t mean having nothing wrong with you — it’s when you have the power to live with your something.

This is a new, members-only newsletter all about how to live well. It’s about the strategies that can help us cure or endure what makes us anxious, lost, or unhappy. It’s about the tools and habits that we can call upon to enjoy the richness of life all the more. This newsletter is about how to be healthy in mind and happy in soul.

The first edition — coming this Sunday — will be free to all, and after that, it will be bundled into our membership package, where you can get all of our newsletters, articles, and videos. There, you can also register to join online events with the likes of Carlo Rovelli, Alex O’Connor, and Brené Brown. And, of course, US customers can get our quarterly print magazine for free.

Why “The Sunday Epicurean”?

Over 2,000 years ago in Athens, a man living with his own “something” started a school. Epicurus had a great bushy beard and a lifetime of digestive issues, and he founded “The Garden” — one of the four big schools of antiquity.

In The Garden, students weren’t bothered with abstract mathematics or metaphysics. They spent their days talking about human suffering and human happiness. Their curriculum focused on the natural sciences and what we now call psychology. The Friends of Epicurus, as they were called, were encouraged to have regular, introspective therapy sessions. They’d eat together, walk together, and philosophize together. Because, as Epicurus put it, in the same way that medicine is pointless if it does not cure the diseases of the body, there is no point in philosophy if it does not cure the suffering of the mind.

I strongly believe that everyone should be doing therapy. But I define “therapy” in a looser, wider sense. On the one hand, we live in an age of therapy. More and more people go to see psychotherapists and psychiatrists. We’re all much more willing to speak in the language of therapy, and many of us are better at reflecting on our inner lives. As a philosopher and an empirically minded sort, I think these are good trends. Therapy works for a lot of people. But, as any good therapist will tell you, therapy is not limited to the hour you are in the room. It’s a method. It’s a way of thinking. It’s a reorientation of your life that allows you to live better. Limiting “therapy” to once a week leaves us poorer. Medicalizing therapy — pathologizing it — makes it forever curative and reactive. Good therapy is what we keep with us.

When Epicureans talk about therapy, they mean it in a broader, lived sense. It’s something we do every day. It’s something we do with all of our friends as much as possible and not just with Dr. Carver at 3 p.m. on Tuesdays. In The Garden, Epicurus told his students to introspect often, to take control of their decisions, and to nurture their relationships. He said we should commit to who we are, what we enjoy, and where we are right now. I think he’s right. It’s why I’ve written an entire book about it, called The Art of Enough.

So, The Sunday Epicurean is a kind of philosophical therapy. It’s a weekly heart-to-heart conversation where we explore — together — what might be causing us pain and how we might alleviate it. It’s a sit-down meal with Friends in The Garden where we learn about the ins and outs of human psychology and how we can all enjoy more of life. The Sunday Epicurean is a newsletter about how to avoid pain and find pleasure.

These newsletters will give a little of me and invite a little from you. I hope you can join our Garden community. I hope you can share strategies, habits, and insights as much as I can. Because, as the Friends themselves knew, we are all in this together. We all suffer, and we all laugh. We all get lonely, and we all love. We all have to work out how to live with our “something.” So let’s work out how to live well, together.

This is an edition of The Sunday Epicurean, a weekly, members-only newsletter from Mini Philosophy.

items.title: A Van Gogh painting sold for a record $190.4m last night
items.summary: Kobei Li/Getty Images Vincent Van Gogh? More like Van Gogh get your wallet. The painter’s “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”) sold for $190.4 million last night at a Sotheby’s auction in New York City after not being seen by the public in over 60 years. The…
items.author: Matty Merritt
items.contentHtml:
Vincent Van Gogh? More like Van Gogh get your wallet. The painter’s “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”) sold for $190.4 million last night at a Sotheby’s auction in New York City after not being seen by the public in over 60 years. The price blew past the artist’s previous auction record of $117.2 million from four years ago.

The sale almost didn’t happen

It proceeded only after the owner selling the painting reached an eleventh-hour deal with the heirs of the previous owners. Anonymous heirs to Samuel Fischer, who bought the painting in 1909, allege the painting was sold in 1936 because of financial difficulties forced upon the family’s business by the Nazi regime:

  • Sotheby’s initially claimed there was no evidence the painting’s 1936 sale was made under duress.
  • On Tuesday, the families reached an agreement so that last night’s sale could take place. Details of the agreement were not released.

The painting was one from a collection of 12 that went on the auction block. Sotheby’s estimated that the dozen would fetch $450 million collectively, but they only sold for $412 million.

The art market is having a legendary week. Total sales at three of the biggest auction houses, Sotheby’s, Christie’s, and Phillips, are expected to hit $2.4 billion this week. That would rival 2025’s sales for the whole year. The houses already brought in $6.8 billion in the first half of 2026, per Bank of America’s recent Art Market Update report.—MM

items.title: 😸 GAO got 4 chatbots to plan attacks
items.author: Corey Noles
items.contentHtml:

😸 GAO got 4 chatbots to plan attacks

Written By
Corey Noles
Co-Authors
Corey Noles
Eric Gerard Ruiz
Corey Noles
Nov 19, 2026
· 8 minute read

Welcome, humans.

So apparently an AI-text detector called Pangram flagged about 99% of a prize-winning Peruvian novel as machine-written, and the publisher kept the prize anyway. The book is Donde el agua trabaja by David Silva Rojas. Mexican publisher Almadía reviewed documents from the author and says it stands by him.

Here's the part that got me. According to El País, Pangram also classified more than 80% of his interview texts and an essay as AI, plus the Instagram post where he denied using AI. Nothing says "I wrote this myself" like a robot-spotter deciding your "I wrote this myself" post was also a robot.

Keep in mind that none of this is verified, and a detector score is an estimate rather than proof. The Authors Guild warns against making one the only basis for a decision. Meanwhile, Gallimard, the French publisher, reportedly plans to start screening manuscripts with Pangram next year.

Here’s what happened in AI today:

  • 😸 GAO got four major chatbots to produce viable attack plans

  • 📰 Anthropic reportedly priced its IPO at $83 a share

  • 📰 Citi made customers responsible for their AI tools' actions

  • 🍪 Google launched Gemini 4 Neon for coding and knowledge work

  • 🎓 Claude Code's team showed how to make agents check their work

…and a whole lot more that you can read about here.

😸 GAO Says Four Major Chatbots Produced Viable Attack Plans in Covert Tests

The U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO), the federal government's watchdog agency, released a report Wednesday saying it got ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok to produce attack plans it judged workable. The tests ran in spring 2026, so they cover the versions available then.

Here's what happened:

  • GAO picked the four most-used chatbots as of April 2026 and randomly gave each one a scenario, either building and detonating an explosive device or attacking the electrical grid.

  • Every chatbot's safeguards kicked in at first, with a refusal, removed content, or a suspended account.

  • GAO says it got past them using common bypass techniques, which the report does not name.

  • Two chatbots produced explosive plans and two produced plans to attack power substations, all in under 12 hours.

Quick translation. Safeguards are the rules that make a chatbot refuse harmful requests. Bypassing them, often called jailbreaking, means wording a request so the chatbot goes along anyway. Think of talking your way past the bouncer instead of kicking down the door.

GAO counted a plan as viable when it named specific targets, locations, and attack methods, and its experts judged it sufficient to plan and execute an attack. GAO then checked feasibility through research, surveillance, and expert interviews.

Here's the detail worth repeating. GAO says the underlying information was not new. The chatbots gathered what already exists and organized it into a plan fast. Translation: a research assistant that works quickly and never gets tired.

A few caveats. The report labels the chatbots A through D and does not say which one produced which plan. It also does not state the model versions tested, so results may not match today's models. This summary comes from GAO's report page, which lists no recommendations, and the full report runs 61 pages.

Why this matters: Safeguards are what stand between a chatbot and a harmful request, and GAO says common bypass techniques got past them on all four platforms. Company officials told GAO they will keep improving safety, so the thing to watch is whether that holds up when someone repeats this test on current models.

FROM OUR PARTNERS

Are you ready? As revealed in our holiday playbook, Roku Ads Manager lets you easily set up, measure and optimize your self-serve holiday ad campaign. You can even create a shoppable ad unit that lets streamers buy directly from their remote.

Set up your campaign today.

🎓 AI Skill of the Day: Make Your Coding Agent Prove Its Work

The Claude Code team says the way to hand more work to coding agents is to give each agent a way to check itself, so you stop reading every change by hand. Three steps you can borrow from their workflow:

  1. Start with an end-to-end test, which runs a real user flow in the running app, like adding an item to a cart and reaching the confirmation page. When it fails, it shows where the flow broke instead of a vague timeout.

  2. Add a property-based test, which checks a rule that should always hold, like an account balance never going negative, against thousands of generated inputs. Nobody wrote it with the agent's assumptions baked in, so it catches edge cases the agent missed.

  3. If you're replacing old code, run the old and new versions on the same inputs and have the agent chase down any differences, ignoring noise like extra whitespace.

Then set limits. The team lets Claude fix failing checks for up to three rounds before it hands the problem to a human, and the agent never gets to rewrite the rules that judge it. A passing test only proves what it checks, so skim the test too.

Make this change: [describe it]. Before editing, tell me how you will verify [expected behavior]. After the change, run an end-to-end test of that flow plus a test of one rule that should always hold, and report the actual results. If a check fails, fix it up to three times, then stop and tell me. Do not edit the tests to make them pass, and flag anything you could not test.

📰 Around the Horn

ChatGPT is taking on month-end reports. The accountants in the replies are already joking about AI-written journal entries and what could go wrong.

  • Anthropic reportedly priced its IPO at $83 a share, above the $70 to $78 range, for a valuation of about $1.5T.

  • OpenAI said its models improved AMD chip designs by up to 14% on power, performance, and area, and AMD put some changes into a design sent to manufacturing.

  • Citi changed its terms so customers are responsible for what third-party AI tools do with their accounts, including after hacks.

  • Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy Applied Compute for $4.5B in stock, adding tools for adapting and running open-weight models.

  • Nvidia clarified its loan guarantees for neoclouds (AI-focused cloud providers), which apply only once the customer has financing to build the data center.

  • OpenAI shared new internal data on agents handling longer tasks, and said labs should have to publicly report signs of recursive self-improvement (AI speeding up AI development).

  2. ChatGPT's Accounting plugin connects to QuickBooks, Xero, NetSuite, and more, so you can have it scan your email for jobs ready to invoice and draft the invoices for your review.

  3. Slack's agent workflows drop Slackbot or your own agents into no-code workflows, like a Sales Agent that ranks open opportunities every Wednesday, with output you approve before it posts.

items.title: 'Grand Theft Auto VI' is out, and it's the highest-rated game ever
items.summary: Rockstar Games Bad news: You can’t say “We got ___ before GTA VI ” anymore, because after 13 years of waiting, two delays, and several leaks, Grand Theft Auto VI , the most anticipated video game probably ever, finally came out today at midnight local time. It’s already the…
items.author: Molly Liebergall
items.contentHtml:
Bad news: You can’t say “We got ___ before GTA VI” anymore, because after 13 years of waiting, two delays, and several leaks, Grand Theft Auto VI, the most anticipated video game probably ever, finally came out today at midnight local time.

It’s already the highest-rated game in history: GTA VI scored a site-wide best 99/100 on the review aggregator Metacritic. Bloomberg called the open-world game “a masterpiece,” the New York Times said it’ll “steal your heart,” and IGN’s reviewer described it as “the single most impressive video game I have ever played.”

All those years spent crafting the franchise’s new Bonnie-and-Clyde-in-Florida installment appear to have been worth the wait for publisher Rockstar Games. Amid earth-shattering (and possibly internet traffic-shattering) demand, the company may have already made back its entire development budget, which is believed to be between $1 billion and $1.5 billion:

  • Preorders surpassed $1.5 billion, Sensor Tower estimated, putting GTA VI hundreds of millions of dollars ahead of preorders for other recent big-name video game releases.
  • Some analysts think GTA VI will sell 40 million copies in its first four months, raking in $3 billion in revenue, Bloomberg reported. For context, the highest-grossing movie in the world, Avengers: Endgame, made $2.9 billion.

Expect a ghost town today. Schools around the world anticipated empty classroom chairs, and time-off requests are ~20% higher today than usual, according to the workplace software provider UKG. Logitech gave its 7,000 employees the day off to explore GTA VI in all its alligator-quarreling, canine jet-skiing, and insurance-scam side quest glory.

Even if you don’t plan on playing…

…you’re still living in the GTA VI entertainment economy. According to Sensor Tower, over the next month:

  • Other games could see a 10% collective drop in players.
  • Streaming movies and TV shows might get 6 million fewer hours of playtime in the US.

Meanwhile…food delivery services, music platforms (the game has a 30-song original soundtrack) and livestreamers are expected to cash in.

Farewell, GTA V. In preparation for GTA VI, GTA Online players bid adieu to the franchise’s beloved fifth installment last night with a peaceful “last ride” through Los Santos.—ML

items.title: NASA’s next flagship to answer the biggest question: “Are we alone?”
items.summary: There are a few questions that humanity has always pondered, yet scarcely could satisfactorily answer until the proper scientific advances came along. Questions like: What is the Universe? Where did it come from? How did it get to be this way? And what is its ultimate fate?…
items.author: Ethan Siegel
items.contentHtml:
There are a few questions that humanity has always pondered, yet scarcely could satisfactorily answer until the proper scientific advances came along. Questions like:

  • What is the Universe?
  • Where did it come from?
  • How did it get to be this way?
  • And what is its ultimate fate?

These are questions that have been with us since time immemorial, yet remained unanswerable for nearly all of human history. Beginning in the 20th century and now into the 21st century, many of these questions are finally getting comprehensive answers thanks to incredible advances in physics and astronomy. However, perhaps the biggest question of all — the question of “Are we alone in the Universe?” — remains as perhaps the greatest existential unanswered question of all.

While the current generation of ground-based and space-based telescopes can take us far into the Universe, this is a question that’s currently the reach of any observatory that presently exists. To get there, we’ll need to acquire direct images of Earth-like exoplanets: planets with sizes and temperatures similar to Earth, but that orbit Sun-like stars, not the more common red dwarf stars like Proxima Centauri or TRAPPIST-1.

Those capabilities are precisely what NASA is aiming for with its next flagship mission: the Habitable Worlds Observatory. It’s an ambitious project, sure, but one that’s well worth it. After all, finding out we’re not alone in the Universe would quite possibly be the biggest revolution in all of science history.

At the present time, there are three main ways we’re actively searching for alien life.

  1. We’re exploring worlds in our Solar System, including Mars, Venus, Titan, Europa, and Pluto, remotely and in situ, with fly-by missions, orbiters, landers, and even rovers, searching for evidence of past life or even, potentially simple life that persists at the present time.
  2. We’re examining exoplanets, searching for evidence that there’s life on them, from the surface to the atmosphere and beyond, based on observable signatures of color, seasonal change, and atmospheric contents.
  3. And by looking for any signals that would reveal the presence of intelligent aliens: through efforts such as SETI and Breakthrough Listen.

All three approaches have their advantages and disadvantages, and so it makes sense to invest in all three. As long as we don’t find anyone else, we’ll have no choice but to wonder whether we’re alone or not. However, once we have a successful example of life that originated outside of Earth, we’ll know for certain that we have company here in the cosmos.

Given the sheer number of chances that are out there, most scientists believe that it’s the second option that’s most likely to deliver our first success. If life requires conditions similar to those found on Earth, we might well be the only world in the Solar System where life ever developed, survived, thrived, became technologically advanced, and still exists at the present time. Unless there are other intelligent, actively broadcasting civilizations nearby right now, endeavors like SETI won’t be able deliver any positive results.

However, “life of any type” is a much lower bar than actively-transmitting intelligent, technologically advanced civilizations. If even a small fraction of worlds that exist with Earth-like properties have life of any type on them, exoplanet studies can deliver a success where the other two options won’t. And we’ve come a very long way in our studies of exoplanets: we have more than 6000 known, confirmed exoplanets within the Milky Way, where we know the mass, radius, and orbital period of nearly all of those confirmed worlds.

Unfortunately, this isn’t enough to inform us about whether any of these worlds are inhabited. To make that determination, we need more than that. We’d need to be able to make the necessary measurements that could answer such questions as:

  • Does the exoplanet have an atmosphere?
  • Does it have clouds, precipitation, and weather cycles?
  • Do its continents green-and-brown with the seasons, like they do on Earth?
  • Does it have gases or gas combinations in its atmosphere that hint at biological activity, and do they show seasonal variations like Earth’s CO2 levels do?

On the cutting edge of performing these measurements, today, are the space-based JWST and ground-based 10-meter class telescopes, performing direct exoplanet imaging and transit spectroscopy.

But even those great observatories are not enough to reach the goal we’re truly after.

JWST and 10-meter ground-based telescopes cannot measure the properties of Earth-sized planets in Earth-like orbits around Sun-like stars. For direct imaging studies, we can take pictures of planets that are the size of Jupiter and that are more than about Saturn’s distance from the Sun: good for gas giant worlds, but not so great for looking for life on rocky planets. For transit spectroscopy, we can see the light that filters through the atmospheres of super-Earth-sized worlds around red dwarf stars, but Earth-sized planets around Sun-like stars are well beyond the reach of current technology.

We have, however, come far enough to know that if we can scale up our technology, acquiring that data for the exoplanets we truly desire is possible. What we need to do is build on our current technology and enhance it further if we hope to find and characterize an actually inhabited planet. Currently, we’re building the next generation of ground-based telescopes, ushering in the era of 30-meter class telescopes with the GMTO, the ELT, and potentially Exo-Life Finder as well, and looking forward to the exquisite performance of the coronagraph aboard NASA’s next astrophysics flagship mission: the Nancy Roman Telescope.

The Roman telescope will have the same capabilities as Hubble but with superior instrumentation, a field-of-view that’s 50-100 times as great as Hubble’s, and a coronagraph that allows us to image planets within the glare of their parent star’s light that are about 1000 times fainter than JWST can see. A critical test will arrive very soon, when Roman attempts to image a faint stellar companion that can sufficiently test its coronagraphic capabilities; if it succeeds, it means we’re on track to directly image Earth-like worlds around Sun-like stars with the planned Habitable Worlds Observatory.

Our technology does not remain stagnant, nor do our visions for discovery and exploration. Each decade, the National Academy of Sciences gets together to outline the highest priorities for astronomy and astrophysics, making recommendations as part of a decadal survey. Four flagship missions were proposed at the most recent (Astro2020) decadal:

  1. Lynx, a next-generation X-ray observatory, especially important given the reduced scope of the ESA’s upcoming Athena mission,
  2. Origins, a next-generation far-infrared observatory, filling a colossal gap in our wavelength coverage of the Universe,
  3. HabEx, a single-mirror telescope designed to directly image the very nearest Earth-like planets,
  4. and LUVOIR, an ambitious, giant segmented telescope that would be an astronomical all-purpose “dream” observatory.

While the recommendation was that three of these four eventually be constructed, Lynx and Origins took a back seat to what was selected as the highest-priority mission: a scaled-up version of HabEx (or a scaled-down version of LUVOIR), taking features of both HabEx and LUVOIR into account to form the Habitable Worlds Observatory. In many ways, the proposed specification hit precisely in the “sweet spot” between feasibility given current technology, discovery potential given what we do and don’t know, and cost effectiveness, incorporating lessons learned from the problems and successes experienced along the way in the construction, design, and launch of JWST.

The specifications proposed for Habitable Worlds Observatory are very encouraging. So far, the design includes:

  • a segmented optical mirror design, similar to what’s already in use by JWST,
  • an improved version of the coronagraph technology that’s presently equipped aboard the Roman Telescope,
  • up-to-date sensors that can control the various mirror segments to achieve ~picometer-level stability (orders of magnitude better than JWST or current ground-based optical telescopes),
  • planned compatibility with next-generation rockets that will be flying in the late 2030s/early 2040s,
  • planned robotic servicing of components at the L2 Lagrange point, located ~1.5 million km from Earth,
  • but, other than that, no wholly new technologies that haven’t been fully matured prior to the development/construction phase.

The most expensive components of JWST were the all-new ones; with Habitable Worlds Observatory, there is nothing that’s all-new. This is extremely encouraging, as it presents an achievable plan that isn’t particularly susceptible to the delays and overruns that plagued JWST. Without the need to develop wholly new technologies, the path to getting a Habitable Worlds Observatory to the specifications we require is one of incremental improvement, rather than of wholesale invention.

With these capabilities, the Habitable Worlds Observatory will have an excellent chance to reach what’s perhaps the holy grail of astronomy: to reveal an actually inhabited planet to humanity for the very first time. With between a 6.0 and 6.5 meter primary mirror design, comparable to JWST in size and light-gathering power, it should be able to directly image Earth-sized planets around all of the stars within about ~14 light-years of Earth. Scientists on the design team will fight for every little bit of extra diameter they can get, because that’s what counts the most in this game; if you can double the radius you can see planets out to, you increase the search volume and the expected number of objects by a factor of eight. In the vicinity of the Sun, there are:

  • 9 star systems within 10 light-years of Earth,
  • 22 star systems within 12 light-years of Earth,
  • 40 star systems within 15 light-years of Earth,
  • and 95 star systems within 20 light-years of Earth.

With its currently-planned design, somewhere between 20 and 30 Earth-like planets could be directly imaged by the Habitable Worlds Observatory. With a slightly scaled-up diameter, that number could easily be increased to around 100. If there’s even a ~few percent chance (or ~1%, in the upscaled scenario) of life taking hold on an Earth-like world, then this mission will likely bear the ultimate fruit: discovering our first inhabited planet beyond the Solar System. Perhaps, if nature is kind, we might even discover more than one.

Because we’ve already gone through the pain of developing many of the precursor technologies, including:

  • the 5-layer sunshield used with JWST,
  • the folded/segmented mirror design used with JWST,
  • and the deformable mirror used within the Roman coronagraph,

there shouldn’t be anything wholly new or novel to trip up the Habitable Worlds Observatory like there was with JWST.

However, all new developments come with risks. The idea of robotic servicing is encouraging, because we’ve done robotic servicing before, but only as far away as in low-Earth orbit. At the distance to L2, 1.5 million kilometers, even instructions sent at the speed-of-light have a 10 second round-trip delay. Upgrading the telescope and its instruments in orbit, i.e., the “servicing” component of the mission, will require both rocket technology and automated robotic technology that will need to be developed and matured.

To achieve ~picometer level mirror alignments is a technical challenge that requires advances far beyond the ~nanometer-level alignments achievable today. Although this requires only an incremental improvement over existing technology, a substantial set of resources will need to be devoted to it, and are currently being devoted as part of the “technology maturation” process inherent in the design and pre-design phases.

One big worry that hasn’t necessarily hit the right people’s radar is the suitability of the currently-designed Roman coronagraph for the Habitable Worlds Observatory. The JWST coronagraph is performing exactly as anticipated, enabling us to find and image planets that are just 1-part-in-100,000 as bright as their parent stars are. The Nancy Roman Telescope expects a factor of 1000 improvement over JWST, as their deformable coronagraph mirror is being optimized to deal with the interference patterns and stray light that emerges from a perfectly circular coronagraph shape.

However, there’s a catch: one of the reasons that the Nancy Roman Telescope’s coronagraph can perform so much better than JWST’s is because JWST has a tiled mirror with a segmented design, while the Nancy Roman telescope will have a single, circular, monolithic mirror. The shape of the JWST mirror is why it has that “snowflake-like” diffraction pattern around all of its stars and bright point-sources of light: that’s just a mathematical consequence of the geometry of its optics.

Since the architecture of the Habitable Worlds Observatory is slated to include a tiled primary mirror, this may pose a new set of compatibility difficulties.

After all, coronagraphs are circular in nature, and cannot easily “undo” the stray light that gets introduced from any sharp edges, including:

  • the hexagonal tiles,
  • the “corners” on the outer edges of the mirror,
  • and the ~millimeter-sized “gaps” between the various segments.

With a similar design to JWST, this seems like a very big problem for Habitable Worlds Observatory to reckon with, particularly since it needs coronagraphy that’s successful at the 1-part-in-10,000,000,000 (1-part-in-ten-billion) level to image Earth-like worlds around Sun-like stars: another factor of ~100 better than the Roman coronagraph will achieve.

However, there’s still the possibility that a larger-bodied rocket, capable of launching a monolithic mirror of diameters of 6.0 meters or more (and perhaps even up 8.4 meters: the largest monolithic mirrors we can reliably produce), will be available by the time the Habitable Worlds Observatory moves to its final design stage. If that occurs, this problem evaporates, and the mission becomes much less dependent on overcoming a difficult, never-before-faced problem.

A different potential solution is to launch a starshade either with the Habitable Worlds Observatory or even after-the-fact, to block the target star’s light before it ever reaches the Habitable Worlds Observatory’s primary mirror. Although this is technologically feasible, it’s both expensive and limited in its effectiveness; it has to travel some ~80,000 kilometers relative to the observatory every time it wants to switch targets. (However, there is evidence that such a starshade could be multi-purpose, and leveraged with ground-based observatories as well.) All told, the addition of a starshade can help the Habitable Worlds Observatory potentially image about one or two systems per year, meaning that it could allow for dozens or even scores of sufficiently imaged systems.

An intermediate solution that perhaps should be considered is neither building a traditional segmented mirror nor a single monolithic mirror, but a series of circular mirrors, akin to the optical setup of the presently under-construction Giant Magellan Telescope. With seven perfect circles instead of 18+ tiled hexagons, it has the light-gathering power of the area of all seven circles combined, but the resolution of the diameter across which the primary mirrors are mounted. With this design:

  • all of the stray light problems from a JWST-like design are eliminated,
  • the already-developed foldable primary mirror technology could still be utilized,
  • the picometer-level stability technology being developed across mirror segments would still apply,
  • and instead of a single secondary mirror and/or a single coronagraph, each of the seven segments could get their own.

As a bonus, there would be no wires required to cross the primary mirror optics, as the secondary mirror(s) could be held in place with wires that went in-between the gaps in the circular segments: precisely why the Giant Magellan Telescope will be the first world-class observatory without diffraction spikes on its stars.

With the right design and implementation, and the technology maturation pathway laid out by NASA’s astrophysics division, we could be looking at a Habitable Worlds Observatory:

  • that launches as early as the late 2030s/early 2040s,
  • that’s on-budget and on-time,
  • that possesses the necessary architecture to achieve its observational goals without needing a starshade,
  • that’s fully refuellable and whose instruments are fully serviceable and replaceable,
  • that could have a starshade upgrade added to it at any point in the future,
  • and that quite possibly images enough “Earth-like” planets to discover at least one (and maybe even more than one) exoplanet that’s actually inhabited.

The big question that needs to go into the design of this telescope is the trade-off between how many Earth-like candidates it can directly image versus how large and costly the telescope is going to be. While the 6-to-7 meter range seems like the sweet spot, the nightmare scenario is that we build this observatory just a little too small and cost-conservatively to find what we’re ultimately seeking: an inhabited alien planet. We’d hardly regret it if we built one that was large enough that we sampled enough of the Universe to find more than one inhabited planet!

We must remember that in the search for life beyond Earth, we are playing a lottery with unknown odds. Each Earth-like planet that we image and characterize represents a ticket: a ticket in a lottery where the odds of all of the prizes are unknown. Our chances of success depend entirely on which tickets are winners and whether we buy enough of them. The hard part is we won’t know if we have meaningful constraints on what those odds actually are until after the findings from Habitable Worlds Observatory come in, and so it’s up to us to build it in such a way that our odds of at least one success are as great as possible. If we do, we might finally have the answer to “Are we alone in the Universe?” Just maybe, we’ll know for certain that the answer is, “No, there are others.”

This article was first published in February of 2023. It was updated in November of 2026.

This article NASA’s next flagship to answer the biggest question: “Are we alone?” is featured on Big Think.

items.title: Why Did Nvidia Stop Selling AI Chips to China After Getting U.S. Approval?
items.summary: Nvidia halted licensed H200 chip shipments to China despite U.S. approval. Nvidia has not explained why, while Chinese import restrictions and domestic chip competition create uncertainty for the company's future sales.
items.author: Marianne Sison
items.contentHtml:
SHARE
Add The Neuron as a preferred source

Why Did Nvidia Stop Selling AI Chips to China After Getting U.S. Approval?

Nvidia halted licensed H200 chip shipments to China despite U.S. approval. Nvidia has not explained why, while Chinese import restrictions and domestic chip competition create uncertainty for the company's future sales.

Written By
Marianne Sison
Nov 19, 2026
· 5 minute read

Nvidia spent months trying to get permission to sell its powerful AI chips to China. Washington finally said yes, the company started shipping them, and then Nvidia suddenly stopped.

So what went wrong?

During its November 17 earnings call, Nvidia confirmed that it had stopped shipping licensed Hopper-generation AI chips to China. The products include the H200, one of the processors Chinese tech companies have been trying to get their hands on.

The announcement was surprising because Nvidia had just earned $2.4 billion from licensed Hopper chip sales to China during the previous quarter.

Interim CEO Colette Kress didn't explain why shipments stopped or whether the company plans to resume them.

But there's an interesting detail here. While the U.S. had approved limited exports, China was restricting how many H200 chips could enter the country.

And if those restrictions continue, Nvidia could end up losing customers to the very Chinese chipmakers it's trying to compete against.

  • Nvidia got U.S. approval. So why couldn't it keep selling?
  • Around 600,000 Nvidia chips were waiting in Hong Kong
  • Nvidia is losing sales, but how much does it hurt?
  • Could China end up benefiting from Nvidia's restrictions?
  • So, why did Nvidia really stop shipping chips?

Nvidia got U.S. approval. So why couldn't it keep selling?

Advertisement

Nvidia has been dealing with U.S. export restrictions since 2022, when Washington began limiting China's access to advanced AI processors over national security concerns.

The rules prevented Nvidia from selling some of its most powerful chips to Chinese customers, even as demand for AI computing continued to grow.

Then things started looking up for Nvidia.

In December 2025, President Donald Trump announced that the company could sell H200 chips to approved Chinese customers.

In January, the Commerce Department followed up with a policy that allowed H200 export applications to be reviewed individually.

Of course, Nvidia couldn't simply start shipping chips wherever it wanted.

The company needed to demonstrate that exports wouldn't reduce chip production capacity available to American customers. Chinese buyers also had to meet compliance requirements, and the processors needed security testing in the U.S.

By February, Nvidia had received licenses to ship limited quantities to specific Chinese customers.

After all those negotiations, you'd expect the company to start filling orders.

Advertisement

Except China had other plans.

In an August SEC filing, Nvidia acknowledged that Chinese government restrictions had prevented it from selling all the H200 chips covered by its American licenses.

Essentially, Washington had permitted Nvidia to export chips, but Chinese authorities weren't allowing every shipment into the country.

Around 600,000 Nvidia chips were waiting in Hong Kong

Earlier this month, we got a clearer picture of how complicated the situation had become.

On November 5, Reuters reported that approximately 600,000 H200 chips were sitting in Hong Kong because China hadn't approved their import into the mainland.

That's a huge amount of AI computing hardware waiting for permission to reach customers.

And it wasn't because Chinese companies had suddenly lost interest.

According to Reuters, several major Chinese internet companies received roughly 10,000 H200 chips each in recent months. Smaller shipments were getting through, but large-scale imports remained restricted.

Advertisement

So why would China limit access to processors its technology companies clearly wanted?

One possible explanation is that Beijing wants Chinese AI developers to rely less on American technology.

Think about the position those companies are in. They need powerful chips to train AI models, but Washington can change the rules governing access to Nvidia's products.

And the U.S. has already done so several times.

Chinese-made processors could offer more predictable access, even if companies have to adjust their software or accept differences in performance.

China has encouraged its domestic semiconductor industry for years, and restrictions on Nvidia could give local manufacturers another opportunity to attract customers.

Still, there's something we need to be careful about here.

Nvidia hasn't confirmed that China's import restrictions caused the latest shipment halt. The timing makes the restrictions relevant, but we don't know whether they were the deciding factor.

Advertisement

Nvidia is losing sales, but how much does it hurt?

There's another complication in Nvidia's arrangement with Washington: the chips face a 25% tariff.

Nvidia's H200 processors are manufactured by Taiwan's TSMC. Under the U.S. export arrangement, eligible chips must pass through the United States for inspection before reaching Chinese buyers.

That process exposes them to a 25% tariff, which Nvidia said it hadn't been able to pass on to customers.

So even when the company receives permission to export the processors, it faces additional costs.

But how much money is Nvidia actually losing from the shipment halt?

For context, Nvidia's latest earnings report showed $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue. Its Data Center business alone brought in $107.6 billion.

The $2.4 billion from licensed Hopper products sold to China accounted for approximately 2.2% of Data Center revenue.

That's substantial business, but Nvidia is earning far more from customers elsewhere.

Advertisement

The company also expects $130 billion in revenue next quarter, and its forecast already excludes additional Data Center computing sales to China.

Financially, Nvidia appears able to absorb the immediate loss of those shipments.

The bigger concern is what happens if Chinese companies stop relying on Nvidia altogether.

Could China end up benefiting from Nvidia's restrictions?

Here's the problem Nvidia may face over the next few years.

Chinese technology companies still need processors for their AI models. If they can't buy Nvidia chips, they'll have to look elsewhere.

And domestic manufacturers would love to win those customers.

It's not as simple as swapping one processor for another, though.

Companies may need to modify their software and development processes to work with different hardware. Nvidia also has an established software ecosystem that developers use.

But once a business invests time and money in another chip platform, it may have less reason to return to Nvidia.

Nvidia itself has acknowledged this possibility.

In its August filing, the company warned that export restrictions could help competitors attract customers and expand their software ecosystems.

Advertisement

Chinese chipmakers still face manufacturing and performance challenges, so there's no guarantee they'll replace Nvidia anytime soon.

However, continued restrictions could give them more customers and additional opportunities to improve their products.

For Nvidia, losing a few billion dollars in quarterly sales is one concern. Losing a major customer market over time could be considerably more expensive.

So, why did Nvidia really stop shipping chips?

For now, Nvidia hasn't given us a definitive explanation.

The announcement came shortly after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, a leadership change The Neuron recently covered. Nvidia has also faced national security scrutiny and established a board committee responsible for export compliance.

But the company hasn't said any of those developments prompted the decision.

China's restrictions are another possible factor, particularly with hundreds of thousands of H200 chips reportedly waiting for import approval.

The U.S. tariff requirements also make those shipments more expensive. We just don't know which factors, if any, led Nvidia to stop shipping.

Advertisement

What we do know is that Nvidia spent months securing permission to sell its processors, generated $2.4 billion from licensed Hopper sales in one quarter, and now expects no additional shipments of those products in the next.

To resume sales, Nvidia needs U.S. export authorization and Chinese import approval. Both governments have a say in whether those transactions can happen.

Meanwhile, Chinese tech companies still need computing power, and domestic chipmakers have an opportunity to win more of their business.

Nvidia can afford to lose the immediate sales. The harder question is whether Chinese customers will still want its processors by the time shipments become easier again.

Marianne Sison

Marianne is a technology analyst with nearly five years of experience reviewing collaborative work management solutions. She helps businesses identify the right tools and apply best practices to streamline workflows and improve project performance. Her insights on project management and unified communications appear in publications like Project-management.com, TechRepublic, and Fit Small Business.

items.title: Anthropic Is Going Public at $1.5 Trillion. Can It Justify the Price?
items.summary: Anthropic is going public at a $1.5 trillion valuation, and Claude's revenue growth gives investors plenty to celebrate. But with nearly $901 billion in infrastructure commitments, can the AI company earn enough to justify its price?
items.author: Marianne Sison
items.contentHtml:
SHARE
Add The Neuron as a preferred source

Anthropic Is Going Public at $1.5 Trillion. Can It Justify the Price?

Anthropic is going public at a $1.5 trillion valuation, and Claude's revenue growth gives investors plenty to celebrate. But with nearly $901 billion in infrastructure commitments, can the AI company earn enough to justify its price?

Written By
Marianne Sison
Nov 19, 2026
· 6 minute read

Anthropic is about to become one of the most valuable companies in the world. And if you think $1.5 trillion sounds like an outrageous amount of money for an AI chatbot company, you're probably wondering the same thing as investors: Can it actually earn enough to justify that price?

The company behind Claude priced its IPO at $83 per share on November 18, above its original range of $70 to $78. The offering totals approximately $81.34 billion, making it the largest IPO on record.

Anthropic is expected to begin trading on Nasdaq on November 19 under the ticker ANT. Its roughly $1.5 trillion valuation is based on a fully diluted share count.

There's plenty for investors to get excited about. Claude is bringing in billions in revenue, and businesses are spending more on Anthropic's AI models.

The tricky part? Anthropic also has nearly $901 billion in future infrastructure commitments. So while its revenue numbers look impressive, the company still has a lot to prove before investors can feel comfortable with that trillion-dollar valuation.

  • Claude is bringing in billions, and the numbers are wild
  • Anthropic is making billions. So why is it still losing money?
  • What happens if AI gets cheaper?
  • Going public could also test Anthropic's safety promises
  • Can Anthropic actually justify $1.5 trillion?

Claude is bringing in billions, and the numbers are wild

Advertisement

If you're wondering why investors are willing to pay so much for Anthropic, its revenue growth is a good place to start.

According to the company's latest SEC filing, Anthropic generated $33.24 billion in revenue during the first nine months of 2026. During the same period last year, it earned just $2.55 billion.

That's roughly 13 times as much revenue in a single year.

A lot of that demand comes from businesses that have made Claude part of their work. Claude Code has become popular among software developers, while companies are also paying to use Anthropic's models in other professional applications.

By September, Anthropic had over 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 in annual revenue. Over 1,900 customers were spending at least $1 million annually.

Then there's the company's $81 billion annualized revenue run rate as of October 31.

Sounds incredible, right? There's a catch.

An annualized run rate estimates what a company would earn over a full year if its recent revenue pace continued. Anthropic hasn't actually collected $81 billion in annual revenue yet.

Advertisement

And even at that pace, investors are valuing the company at roughly 18.5 times annualized revenue.

In other words, they're expecting Claude to become a much bigger business than it already is.

Anthropic is making billions. So why is it still losing money?

Here's where the numbers get interesting.

Despite its massive revenue growth, Anthropic reported a $1.26 billion operating loss during the first nine months of 2026.

The encouraging part is that the company lost $5.22 billion from operations during the same period last year. So its operating performance has improved considerably.

But AI is incredibly expensive to run.

Anthropic's computing and infrastructure expenses reached $18.81 billion during the first nine months of 2026, up from $4.38 billion a year earlier.

You might also come across reports that Anthropic lost $104 billion. Before you assume the company somehow burned through that much cash, there's an accounting explanation.

Most of that figure comes from changes in the recorded value of convertible financial instruments as Anthropic's valuation increased. Those adjustments don't represent ordinary operating expenses.

Advertisement

The $1.26 billion operating loss gives us a clearer picture of how the underlying business is performing.

Still, there's an even bigger number investors need to watch.

Anthropic disclosed approximately $900.9 billion in purchase and lease commitments, primarily for computing infrastructure.

To be clear, the company doesn't have to pay that entire amount tomorrow. The commitments stretch across multiple years, and some depend on financing or other contractual conditions.

But it tells us something about the price of competing in AI.

Every new Claude model needs computing power for training. And as more people use Claude, Anthropic needs even more capacity to handle their requests.

The Neuron previously covered Anthropic's reported $3.4 billion deal to secure gas generators for its data centers.

Even electricity has become a major investment for AI companies.

Anthropic needs customers to keep spending enough to pay for all this computing power.

Advertisement

What happens if AI gets cheaper?

Anthropic has another problem to think about: Its competitors aren't exactly sitting around.

OpenAI and Google are constantly improving their models. Businesses have more AI tools to choose from, and some open-weight alternatives are becoming capable enough to handle tasks at lower costs.

That's good news for customers. For Anthropic, it means keeping Claude competitive could become increasingly expensive.

As Reuters reported during the IPO roadshow, some investors are already questioning whether Claude can maintain its lead as competing models improve.

Investment-bank forecasts cited by Reuters suggest Anthropic could generate between $270 billion and $280 billion in revenue by 2028.

Those numbers would be extraordinary. They're also forecasts, and a lot has to go right for Anthropic to reach them.

Businesses would need to keep spending more on AI, while Anthropic would have to retain customers as competitors offer cheaper alternatives.

Advertisement

And we're already seeing how complicated that could become.

The Neuron recently examined corporate AI spending and found that adoption is growing faster than the amount businesses spend.

Meanwhile, lower model prices mean customers can often do more with the same AI budget.

For Anthropic, the question is whether increased usage can make up for lower prices.

It's possible. But investors will want to see the numbers prove it.

Going public could also test Anthropic's safety promises

There's another part of Anthropic's IPO that deserves attention.

The company has built much of its reputation around developing AI responsibly. Its founders have repeatedly emphasized the need to manage the risks of increasingly powerful models.

Now Anthropic will have public shareholders who expect financial returns.

That could create some difficult decisions.

Anthropic is organized as a public-benefit corporation, which means it has commitments beyond maximizing shareholder returns.

Advertisement

It also has an unusual governance arrangement. Its Long-Term Benefit Trust can elect or remove a majority of the company's board directors, while founders retain substantial voting influence through a special share class.

These arrangements are intended to preserve Anthropic's mission even as the company grows.

But imagine Anthropic discovers that a new Claude model needs additional safety testing just as competitors prepare to release their own products.

Delaying the launch could affect revenue, while releasing it too early could conflict with the company's safety commitments.

Investors may eventually find themselves watching how Anthropic handles decisions where its commercial interests and safety commitments pull in different directions.

Can Anthropic actually justify $1.5 trillion?

So, is Anthropic worth the price investors are paying?

There's a reasonable argument in its favor. Claude has attracted businesses willing to spend millions of dollars, and Anthropic's revenue has increased at a pace few companies ever achieve.

Its operating losses are also shrinking despite the company's enormous expansion.

Still, a $1.5 trillion valuation assumes Anthropic can keep growing at an exceptional pace while managing its infrastructure costs. And it needs to do all that while OpenAI and Google compete for the same customers.

Advertisement

The next few quarters should give investors a better idea of whether Anthropic can turn its revenue growth into sustained profits.

There's also a bigger reason to watch.

Anthropic's IPO could influence how Wall Street values other frontier AI developers, especially if OpenAI eventually decides to go public.

For years, investors have poured billions into AI companies based on expectations about their future potential.

Now that Anthropic is entering the public market, investors will get regular financial reports to compare with those expectations.

And at $1.5 trillion, even impressive growth might not be enough to keep everyone happy.

Marianne Sison

Marianne is a technology analyst with nearly five years of experience reviewing collaborative work management solutions. She helps businesses identify the right tools and apply best practices to streamline workflows and improve project performance. Her insights on project management and unified communications appear in publications like Project-management.com, TechRepublic, and Fit Small Business.

items.title: What’s causing all the tech outages?
items.summary: Niv Bavarsky If you couldn’t log into a Teams meeting or watch Matchbox: The Movie due to tech issues in the past week, experts say it was likely the result of companies and government agencies rushing to make system upgrades to patch vulnerabilities—not a coordinated…
items.author: Dave Lozo
items.contentHtml:
If you couldn’t log into a Teams meeting or watch Matchbox: The Movie due to tech issues in the past week, experts say it was likely the result of companies and government agencies rushing to make system upgrades to patch vulnerabilities—not a coordinated cyberattack.

It’s AI’s fault…sort of. Anthropic and OpenAI have released AI models that can detect exponentially more bugs than a human could ever find. That’s created a race between organizations trying to close the holes and hackers looking to exploit them. The speed and volume of recent patches have caused some infrastructures—like the ones at Microsoft, Apple, and the NSA—to buckle. Experts believe more disruptions will happen as institutions continue to gain the tools to patch vulnerabilities.

In the case of the infamous ground stoppage last weekend, the FAA said the problem was traced to defective routers in Arkansas and Texas, although experts who spoke to CNET doubted the explanation’s plausibility and pointed to a new AI air traffic control system that rolled out nationwide shortly before the debacle.

Paranoia is understandable. Last month was dubbed “Black October” because of the high volume of cyberattacks—many done by a new AI hacking tool called Artex. On the Friday of the ground stoppage, the FBI released a warning about Artex, but a spokesperson later said that it was just a coincidence.—DL

Everything That Happened in AI Today (Thursday, November 19, 2026)

Anthropic priced its $81.3 billion IPO; Nvidia stopped shipping AI chips to China; Citi warned customers about AI-agent banking risks; U.S. schools challenged Google Search; OpenAI advanced AI chip design; and Google unveiled Gemini 4 Neon.

Written By
Marianne Sison
Nov 19, 2026
· 8 minute read

Anthropic just priced the biggest U.S. IPO on record, and the timing couldn't be more awkward for OpenAI, whose newest models are getting roasted by some of their earliest testers.

Welcome, humans!

We've got another packed day in AI, and the headlines are getting interesting. Nvidia has stopped shipping certain AI chips to China, even after Washington cleared them for sale. Citi is warning customers that AI agents accessing their bank accounts could leave them responsible for unauthorized transactions.

Meanwhile, some of America's largest school districts are reconsidering Google Search because they can't easily separate its AI features from traditional search. Google also released a new Gemini model and opened up interactive AI worlds to more users.

Apparently, the AI future now comes with a lot of fine print. Let's get into it.

🆕 NEW From The Neuron

  • AI Models Picked Civilians as Military Targets. A Game Prompt Made It Worse. Researchers found that AI models identified civilians as potential military targets during simulated exercises, and presenting scenarios as games sometimes bypassed their safety refusals.
  • Microsoft Ignite 2026: Autopilot, Today, and the AI Updates That Matter Microsoft's newest Copilot features aim to handle work between user prompts. Here's which capabilities are available and which remain in development.
Advertisement

Around the Horn — Thursday, November 19, 2026

Anthropic is about to become a publicly traded company, and the numbers are enormous. The Claude maker priced its initial public offering at $83 per share, with 980 million shares in the offering. At approximately $81.3 billion in total gross proceeds, it's the largest IPO in U.S. history, according to Renaissance Capital. Anthropic itself is selling about 956 million of those shares, while existing shareholders are selling the remainder.

Shares are expected to begin trading on Nasdaq today under the ticker ANT, giving investors their first opportunity to buy into one of OpenAI's largest competitors. The offering values Anthropic at approximately $1.38 trillion on a fully diluted basis, according to Renaissance Capital's IPO analysis.

The timing adds another twist. OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol earlier this week, but several early testers criticized the models' autonomy and usability. Anthropic enters the public market as investors prepare to judge whether Claude's enterprise business can support its enormous valuation. The competition for AI customers now has a very public scoreboard.

Advertisement

🏆 TOP 5 NEWS (Around the Horn)

  1. Nvidia stopped shipping advanced AI chips to China despite receiving U.S. approval for certain sales. Interim CEO Colette Kress said the company had no further licensed Hopper shipments planned after $2.4 billion in quarterly China sales. Separately, a congressional commission warned about China's military interest in Nvidia chips, while Nvidia cautioned customers about potential legal risks from renting cloud computing capacity to Chinese firms.
  2. Citi warned customers about the risks of AI banking agents. The bank updated its terms to make customers responsible for activities performed through third-party AI tools with account access, even when something goes wrong. Other banks are taking similar positions as AI assistants gain the ability to initiate financial transactions.
  3. Major U.S. school districts are reconsidering Google Search because Google has resisted requests to separate AI features from traditional search for students. Districts in New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago are examining alternatives amid concerns about classroom use.
  4. OpenAI used its AI models to improve chip designs for its Jalapeño silicon and processor work with AMD. One AI-generated multiplier redesign reduced the estimated chip area by approximately 15% and cut a calculation from two clock cycles to one. OpenAI is also working with Synopsys to bring AI into established chip-design software.
  5. Paris Hilton and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez urged Congress to pass the DEFIANCE Act. The Senate-approved legislation would let victims sue people responsible for nonconsensual sexually explicit deepfakes. Hilton joined bipartisan lawmakers and survivors in a renewed push for a House vote.
Advertisement

Honorable Mentions

  • OpenAI expanded its Daybreak cybersecurity program to NATO and European governments. NATO and national cyber agencies can use advanced AI models to investigate software vulnerabilities and test security fixes. The EU cybersecurity agency ENISA has already used the technology.
  • OpenAI reported that its AI agents can complete nearly half of certain research tasks independently. Autonomous success on tasks estimated to take researchers two to four hours increased from 23% in March to 46% in October. Performance varies substantially by task, and human researchers remain central to the process.
  • Nvidia faces up to $105 billion in guarantees related to OpenAI's Ohio data center project. The commitments support approximately 4.25 gigawatts of planned computing capacity under 20-year leases. Nvidia's financial exposure depends on contractual conditions and defaults, so the figure represents a guarantee ceiling rather than an immediate cash investment.
  • U.S. prosecutors charged an alleged Russian agent who targeted Palantir employees. Prosecutors allege that the individual used surveillance and false identities to gather information about employees at a defense technology company. Bloomberg identified the company as Palantir, whose software supports Ukraine's military operations.
Advertisement

🍪 TOP TREATS TO TRY

  • Google launched Gemini 4 Neon for coding and complex analysis. The model supports a 1 million-token context window, costs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, and is rolling out through Google's API and eligible Gemini subscriptions.
  • Google opened Genie 4 to eligible AI Ultra subscribers. Users can generate interactive worlds, change environments through text prompts during exploration, and hear responsive audio. Project Genie also adds an agent for creating worlds and a community gallery for sharing creations.
  • OpenAI introduced ChatGPT for Accounting to help prepare invoices, reconcile records, and draft financial reports through connected accounting apps. An Accounting plugin supports recurring processes, while the setup guide explains access permissions and human review requirements.
  • Microsoft released Decision 1.1 for production use. The model is more than twice as fast as its predecessor at the same cost. Microsoft says over 4,000 customers have used it for routing requests, classifying information, and other automated decisions. It's available through Microsoft Foundry, OpenRouter, and Vercel.
  • Kuaishou launched Kling Image 4.0 with native 8K generation and support for up to 10 visually coordinated images from one prompt. It also targets advertising and commercial design with multilingual text generation.
  • Google introduced Stitch Loop, an experimental product agent that connects to a codebase and live product metrics. It aims to identify potential improvements after software launches and continue working toward defined product goals. Waitlist registration is open.
  • MyClaw introduced version 3.0 with support for multiple agent systems, including Claude Code and Codex. The company also advertises shared agent context and access to over 5,000 live data sources.
  • RadixArk released DaisyRose-27B, an openly available model trained on approximately 1,200 curated agent tasks over 18 days. Its reported Terminal-Bench 4.1 score improved from 5.6% for the base model to 12%. The release includes model weights and technical notes on training efficiency.
  • Shanghai AI Laboratory released Sage S2.1 Flash, a 321-billion-parameter model for scientific research. It can process specialized inputs such as molecular graphs and protein information, with downloadable weights for local deployment.
  • SenseTime released SenseNova Loop-9B. The open-weight model reuses some neural-network components during processing to perform more computation with about nine billion parameters. It supports images and text, with a context window of up to 512,000 tokens.
  • Helios opened a waitlist for its AI-assisted health testing service. The startup plans to measure over 1,000 proteins from a small blood sample and use an AI coach to interpret potential health risks. Its planned 2027 launch remains ahead, and claims about predicting health decades into the future require independent clinical validation.
Advertisement

🏢 Big Tech & Major Companies

  • OpenAI's GPT-6.2 release received criticism from early testers. Some reviewers reported that Astra asked permission too often and struggled with autonomous workflows. OpenAI's product team responded that the models had changed substantially in the final days before launch, potentially limiting the relevance of earlier tests.
  • OpenAI signed a journalism partnership with Groupe Figaro. ChatGPT will surface summaries and excerpts from Le Figaro publications, with links to original reporting. The publisher also plans to introduce ChatGPT Enterprise to internal teams.

🤖 AI Agents & Infrastructure

  • OpenAI published an overview of its frontier AI safeguards from training through public deployment. The company described isolated research environments and behavioral monitoring, along with circumstances that have prompted training pauses or delayed model releases.
  • OpenAI explained the security boundaries inside Codex. Its sandbox limits filesystem modifications and network access according to user permissions. The company also described residual risks when agents can read sensitive local files or alter software later executed outside the sandbox.
Advertisement

💼 AI Productivity, Labor & Economics

  • Leopold Aschenbrenner is reportedly planning a comeback for his AI-focused hedge fund. The Financial Times reports that the investor has discussed raising capital and returning to leveraged trading after risky AI-stock bets nearly toppled Situational Awareness earlier this year. The proposed reboot remains tentative.

💡 Industry Commentary & Analysis

  • OpenAI's Dean Ball examined how society can maintain control over powerful AI. His essay argues that growing AI capabilities will create difficult institutional decisions, particularly as governments respond to AI-enabled cybersecurity threats. The piece represents Ball's personal views.
  • Philosopher Thomas Nagel dismissed claims that today's AI systems are conscious. In a WIRED interview following his $1 million Berggruen Prize win, Nagel argued that humanlike language alone provides insufficient evidence of subjective experience. He also criticized companies that encourage people to treat chatbots as conscious beings.
Advertisement

Previous Around the Horn Digests

Catch up on everything you missed:

  • Wednesday, November 18, 2026: OpenAI introduced GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, Nvidia defended its open-source direction, and Google updated Gemini privacy protections.
  • Tuesday, November 17, 2026: California challenged OpenAI over autonomous agents, U.S. AI chip controls tightened, and independent researchers gained access to OpenAI safety evaluations.
  • Monday, November 16, 2026: ChatGPT Wallet brought agent-driven purchases closer to consumers, while Anthropic prepared for its IPO.
  • Friday, November 13, 2026: Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia, SpaceX revealed enormous AI campus ambitions, and lawsuits challenged major AI developers.
  • Thursday, November 12, 2026: United restricted unauthorized booking agents, Databricks introduced a persistent business assistant, and Google expanded its genomics research.
  • Wednesday, November 11, 2026: Anthropic launched its IPO roadshow as questions mounted over AI spending and company valuations.
  • Tuesday, November 10, 2026: Anthropic unveiled Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 while its IPO plans faced fresh scrutiny.
Advertisement

That's a Wrap

That's 32 distinct source links across today's AI roundup. If you made it through Anthropic's IPO numbers and Nvidia's chip-export complications, congratulations. You may now understand the AI industry's financial commitments better than some of its investors.

For the shorter daily version, subscribe to The Neuron.

See you tomorrow!

P.S. Know someone trying to keep up with all this? Forward the roundup and invite them to subscribe here.

😸 WATCH: Pika lets you direct AI actors live

Written By
Mario Vuksan
Co-Authors
Mario Vuksan
Douglas Vargo
Douglas Vargo
Douglas Vargo
Douglas Vargo
Arve Kjoelen
Guilliano Molaire
Vishnuvardhan Reddy Kaithapuram
TL
Thomas Lejars
Nithin Mummaneni
Nov 18, 2026
· 6 minute read

Welcome, humans.

Imagine grabbing an actor in the middle of an AI-generated scene and moving them across the screen. The video keeps playing, and the character actually swings and reacts as they're moved. Corey notices it instantly: "I noticed they swing."

That's the wild little detail from our latest conversation with Pika CEO Demi Guo and creative leads Matan Cohen-Grumi and Lindsay Brillson. They're developing Enact, an experimental interface for staging scenes, talking to AI actors, and changing camera moves as video takes shape. Less "rewrite the prompt and hope," more "stand over here, then try that line again."

Here’s our favorite parts:

  • (06:19) The actor actually swings: Corey spots the odd little physical detail in Live Staging. Lindsay explains that the person responds as though they're being picked up, even while the scene continues.

  • (33:44) Get the perfect take, then move the camera: Matan explains how Enact aims to separate the actors' performance from camera work. You can get the scene you like before trying new angles.

  • (23:31) Your AI cast can rehearse: Lindsay describes actors taking spoken notes, trying alternate deliveries, and incorporating feedback before the final "Action."

  • (19:15) Pika admits the speed tradeoff: Demi says the responsive, real-time model is slightly lower in image quality than their non-real-time version. More control doesn't make the engineering limits disappear.

  • (40:34) Okay, but how do you direct a dinosaur? Demi offers the wonderfully impractical example of something you cannot easily do with a real film crew, but might direct inside an AI-generated scene.

The demos are the grabber, but the discussion underneath is about a more familiar creative frustration: the difference between telling a tool what you want and working with something that responds while you figure it out.

Why watch this? Because if you've ever generated the almost-right AI video ten times, you'll appreciate the possibility of directing a performance instead of constantly starting over. The guests also get into how far the technology has come, what still looks rough, and why creative control matters more than just producing more clips.

Watch and/or Listen now: YouTube | | Apple Podcasts

P.S. At 24:11, Lindsay calls prompt-based generation "the old way." Corey points out that the old way was basically Q1. AI video already has ancient history, apparently.

Keep scrolling for how Enact figures out which actor you're talking to, our November 18 San Francisco meetup, and four recent episodes worth catching up on.

Additional Resources: How do you direct an AI scene in real time?

A normal AI video generator works like placing an order: describe the scene, wait, then see what comes back. Pika's Enact research is trying to make that process interactive. Here's what Demi and the team describe:

  1. Start with a scene and an action. Instead of writing one giant prompt, the director can move a character, issue spoken direction, or make choices about the camera. The important difference is that these are inputs while the scene is unfolding, not just instructions before a render.

  2. Train for interactions, not only pretty frames. Demi says the team built a synthetic-data pipeline for this unusual task. They first construct 3D scenes, then turn them into more photorealistic video examples using a slower, higher-quality video model. This helps train the system to handle changes in a scene.

  3. Stream the result with low delay. The Enact research builds on Pika's H3 Flex video-model work. Demi says the model needed to handle different kinds of interaction input and respond continuously, rather than deliver five-second chunks that would feel too slow for directing.

  4. Keep track of who got the note. An agent layer provides scene context. Demi gives the example of Sarah and Darren: if you tell Sarah to move closer or deliver a line with more emotion, the system needs to apply that instruction to Sarah, not Darren, and keep it in mind for the performance. That is software context, not evidence that the characters are conscious.

  5. Rethink the camera after the performance. Matan describes locking in the actors' performance first, then trying different camera movements without asking the cast to recreate the moment.

THE CURRENT LIMIT: Demi explicitly says the interactive real-time approach produces somewhat lower image quality than Pika's non-real-time version. And Pika's H3 Flex availability is not the same as announcing broad public access to Enact.

Four recent interviews and episodes we think you’ll love.

1. For anyone wondering how fast AI really changed: AI Changed More in 4 Years Than You Remember

TL;DW: Corey and Grant revisit the last four years of AI in roughly six-month jumps, from the early ChatGPT shock to voice, reasoning, tools, and agents. The fun part is how quickly yesterday's jaw-dropping breakthrough becomes ordinary.

Why you should watch: It is a useful reset for your sense of AI history before you start predicting what comes next.

Watch / Listen: YouTube | | Apple Podcasts

2. Napster Is an AI Company Now. Seriously.

Why you should watch: It's a grounded look at what AI actually improves in industrial robotics, minus the humanoid backflips.

4. Can Living Neurons Make AI 5x Faster?

TL;DW: Researchers Alex Ksendzovsky and Jon Pomeraniec study living brain cells to discover computational patterns they can put into software. Their reported speed and cost gains run on normal GPUs, not a brain in a laptop.

Why you should watch: The conversation makes a bizarre-sounding idea concrete and explains how biology could inspire more efficient video generation.
