items.contentHtml:
How this founder built a better Duolingo with Codex | William Imoh

Listen now on YouTube • • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

  • WorkOS—Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more

  • Vanta—Automate compliance and simplify security

William Imoh is the founder of Hackmamba and the creator of Mural, an AI language tutor he built after a 1,000-day Duolingo streak still left him unable to hold a conversation in Norwegian. In this episode, he shows how he used Codex and GPT-Live to build native iOS and Android apps despite having no Swift or Kotlin experience, and explains how he designed Mural to teach through complete immersion. He also walks through the Lord of the Rings–themed team of Grok Bots that helps him run a 25-person company, from Gandalf as chief of staff to Legolas in marketing and Aragorn in sales.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. When agents write the code, the programming languages you know matter far less. William had never written Swift, but he wanted Mural to feel truly native, so Codex built it in Swift for iOS and Kotlin for Android. The technical stack followed the product vision, not the skills of the founder.

  2. Taste is often just design judgment expressed clearly. William told Codex to create a minimal, Apple-quality app that felt like autumn. When the first version came back in dark mode, he redirected it toward warm colors, gradients, and a lighter visual style.

  3. Product management experience translates directly into better prompting. William structures his requests as epics and user stories tied to specific user problems. That discipline gives the agent clearer goals and consistently produces stronger results.

  4. Real-time voice is finally good enough to build around, but it remains expensive. William says Mural would not have been possible without GPT-Live-1. A 30-minute session costs roughly $3 to $5, which is expensive for software but still cheaper than an on-demand human tutor.

  5. Agents feel more like colleagues when they have clear identities and jobs. William’s Grok Bot team includes Gandalf as chief of staff, Legolas in marketing, Elrond in engineering, and other Lord of the Rings characters across the business. The personas make each agent’s responsibilities easier to understand and delegate to.

  6. Useful context comes from access, not longer prompts. William connected his agents to Google Workspace, Linear, Notion, Pipedrive, QuickBooks, his calendar, and browser tools. He grants broad access by default, while keeping banking and customer data protected.

  7. The future may be custom systems of record with AI on top. William built Three Pipes, an internal HR tool that combines email, calendar, and meeting notes to track and rank candidates. Instead of adapting his workflow to generic software, he created the database his company actually needed.

  8. Better models reduce the need for elaborate skill libraries. Most of William’s skills became unnecessary as the underlying models improved. The few that survived encode durable expertise, including growth strategy, content strategy, and removing AI-style writing.

  9. When an agent stalls, restart with clearer instructions and add a reviewer. William begins a fresh session, breaks the task into steps, and asks the agent to inspect its own work. He also uses Grok Bot to review Cursor’s output.

items.summary: A scene from inside Disfrutar, a previous The 50 winner. Europa Press News/Getty Images Of all the ways for a chef to taste success, being named the world’s best restaurant has to be one of the sweetest. This year, Asador Etxebarri in Atxondo, Spain, gets to Basque in the glory…
items.author: Brendan Cosgrove
items.contentHtml:
Of all the ways for a chef to taste success, being named the world’s best restaurant has to be one of the sweetest. This year, Asador Etxebarri in Atxondo, Spain, gets to Basque in the glory of that honor, according to The 50, a group that highlights top-notch hospitality establishments. But—like the food at grill-happy Asador Etxebarri—the whole process is getting flamed.

Meal ticket: Being included on The 50’s list boosts visibility and revenue, but that’s also part of the problem, since an owner’s focus can get caught up in making the list rather than improving their restaurant. Or, as Ivan Brehm, the chef-owner of Michelin-starred Nouri in Singapore, told CNBC, “Guides and lists now shape the industry they claim to assess.”

Making the list takes effort, too: Ana Roš, whose Hiša Franko restaurant in Slovenia was ranked 60th, opted to skip this year’s best-of event in Lima, Peru, saying the award ecosystem demands significant time, money, and work commitments, like press events and international travel.

It’s not just restaurants: According to finance platform Tide, the average UK worker spends about 2.8 hours per week on self-promotion, which can include vocalizing wins in meetings and writing performative LinkedIn posts that do things like describe brewing a pot of coffee as “optimizing liquidity ratios.”—BC

items.title: Nvidia CEO admits to extramarital affair with suspected Chinese agent
items.summary: Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images Yesterday, Nvidia revealed that it was investigating co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang after he told the board that Alice Huang (no relation), his close business contact whom US intelligence determined to be a spy for the Chinese government, was also…
items.author: Holly Van Leuven
items.contentHtml:
Yesterday, Nvidia revealed that it was investigating co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang after he told the board that Alice Huang (no relation), his close business contact whom US intelligence determined to be a spy for the Chinese government, was also his extramarital affair partner.

In a statement to employees, Jensen Huang said, “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

A company spokesman revealed that Huang would remain in charge during the probe, and its board said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”

Potential ramifications

Lascivious details aside, the situation offers a unique test for the massively valuable semiconductor company. According to Bloomberg:

  • Nvidia’s unconventional organizational structure, designed by Huang—who famously dreamed up his company at a Denny’s—has the CEO overseeing about 60 direct reports tasked with “rapidly implementing his decisions.”
  • Huang has said that keeps the company agile, but it also makes him hard to replace. He has stated publicly that he wants to maintain his role for decades to come.
  • Nvidia doesn’t have a public succession plan, and Huang’s “relentless” schedule means no one is prepared to replace him promptly if the board ever seeks his removal.

This complicates the US–China race for AI supremacy. President Trump has blocked Nvidia’s most advanced chips, Blackwell and Rubin, from entering China. And even before this revelation, Alice Huang’s company, Megaspeed, was investigated by the Commerce Department on suspicion of smuggling the advanced chips into China.

Asked about Huang’s affair last night, President Trump, who has consulted with the Nvidia CEO on AI policy, told reporters, “He has done an amazing job for our country” and that Huang should stay on as CEO.

Big picture: Nvidia is largely seen as the most powerful driver and beneficiary of the AI stock market boom. Last October, it became the first publicly traded company to reach a valuation of $5 trillion.—HVL

items.title: Robbing museums isn’t as lucrative as it seems
items.summary: Kiran Ridley/Getty Images There have been so many high-profile art heists in the last year that you’d think someone put together a super team of thieves to hit museums. And while the art is worth millions, you can’t exactly use a Renoir to buy a meal, so what becomes of these…
items.author: Dave Lozo
items.contentHtml:
There have been so many high-profile art heists in the last year that you’d think someone put together a super team of thieves to hit museums. And while the art is worth millions, you can’t exactly use a Renoir to buy a meal, so what becomes of these works once they’re stolen?

Items with gold can be melted down, and jewel-encrusted objects can be deconstructed and resold, but hocking paintings can be extremely difficult. Interpol and the FBI maintain stolen art databases, which help buyers avoid unwittingly purchasing pilfered merchandise. But the absconders still have options:

  • There’s the black market, where the art can be sold, but often at a fraction of its value.
  • Some thieves will hold art as ransom or use it to negotiate reduced charges on other crimes.
  • Stolen art can be traded for weapons, as was allegedly the case with the Italian mafia.

Once the art is gone, it’s likely gone forever. While two of the four paintings taken from the Renoir Museum this year were dropped right outside its doors, experts say that less than 10% of swiped artwork is ever recovered, with some saying the true number is just 2%–3%, per Euronews.—DL

items.title: People are reading less. But bookstores still thrive
items.summary: Unsplash Despite predictions that e-books would turn paperbacks into fireplace kindling, print editions made up three-quarters of book sales last year, according to the Association of American Publishers. That’s been great for the cozy little shops selling them: The ranks of…
items.author: Sam Klebanov
items.contentHtml:
Despite predictions that e-books would turn paperbacks into fireplace kindling, print editions made up three-quarters of book sales last year, according to the Association of American Publishers. That’s been great for the cozy little shops selling them:

  • The ranks of indie bookstores in the US swelled by 422 last year, up 31% from the previous year, according to the American Booksellers Association.
  • There’s been a proliferation of genre bookstores, specializing in romance novels, horror reads, and more.

Even Barnes & Noble—the bookstore behemoth that spent years struggling to compete with Amazon—is riding high again. A private equity buyout in 2019 installed a veteran bookseller in the CEO role: James Daunt, who instituted decentralized title curation and store redesigns. The revitalized chain planned to add 60 new locations this year after opening dozens of stores in 2025.

Whether it’s through mom-and-pop shops, corporate chains, or the internet, Americans are still buying books:

  • US print book sales in 2025 were up 10% from 2019, though below the pandemic peak in 2021, according to Circana BookScan.
  • Sales growth was led in part by steamy romance novels, while demand for Japanese manga comics surged 40%.

But there’s a reading recession

Algorithmic videos may not be turning us completely into post-literate peasants, but there is some truth to the notion that reading is on the decline.

The share of Americans who read for pleasure on any given day fell from 28% in 2004 to 16% in 2023. And the share of Americans who read short stories or a novel in 2022 fell to 37.6% from 45.2% in 2012, according to federal data.

But reading’s not dead. The share of Americans who at least opened a book of any kind has remained stable since 2013, at 75%, according to the Pew Research Center. And more than a third of US adults read more than five books last year.

Looking ahead: The book industry’s future hinges on getting young people turning pages again, as pleasure-reading among nine- and 13-year-olds is in freefall.—SK

items.title: Investing in art isn’t pragmatic, but there are returns
items.summary: Getty Images A Romantic-era landscape is certainly more pleasant to look at than a framed US Treasury note. But art auction houses and platforms that tout art as a prudent investment warrant the same skepticism as your cousin’s efforts to sell his charcoal drawings on…
items.author: Sam Klebanov
items.contentHtml:
A Romantic-era landscape is certainly more pleasant to look at than a framed US Treasury note. But art auction houses and platforms that tout art as a prudent investment warrant the same skepticism as your cousin’s efforts to sell his charcoal drawings on Instagram.

The biggest dividend is aesthetic satisfaction

Investment experts agree a Rothko isn’t the most efficient way to save for retirement:

  • Art market returns have trailed those of the S&P 500 for much of the past three decades, yielding returns similar to bonds—but with more risk.
  • Art valuations can be more volatile than stocks and arguably even less predictable, as evolving tastes and cultural trends affect the market.
  • Unlike stocks and bonds, paintings and sculptures take time to sell and often incur storage costs.

Economists have also found that art market indexes tend to overestimate returns, as they’re skewed toward more in-demand art pieces getting sold rather than the entire collectibles market.

However…some economists say that the art market has underperformed over the past few years, meaning it might currently be undervalued. Buying art can also be a hedge against financial crashes, since art values often don’t move in sync with the stock market.

You can’t put a price tag on beauty: An art collection is one of the few assets that delivers aesthetic fulfillment and promotes cultural vibrancy, so investment experts advise treating it primarily as a passion.—SK

items.title: The art of running a gallery
items.summary: Unsplash Besides a great excuse to wear black turtlenecks, what do art dealers get out of operating a gallery? Well, if things go right, they can actually make a decent living. But that’s a big “if.” Art-ing from scratch: To start a gallery, you need a place to operate. But…
items.author: Brendan Cosgrove
items.contentHtml:
Besides a great excuse to wear black turtlenecks, what do art dealers get out of operating a gallery? Well, if things go right, they can actually make a decent living. But that’s a big “if.”

Art-ing from scratch: To start a gallery, you need a place to operate. But that’s not cheap: The New York Times reported in 2023 that it cost about $12,000 per month to rent a small-to-midsize gallery in the Big Apple.

Buyers and sellers: Once you’ve got a physical gallery space, you need to start pushing your business’s flywheel: the Rolodex. Building a roster of quality artists attracts big-pocketed collectors, and both are important for gallery owners, who:

  • Either charge artists a flat exhibition fee.
  • Or take a 40%–60% commission on sales, per The Holy Art gallery.

Hidden costs: Even with an affordable studio packed full of trendy art, galleries can struggle to keep those little brass lights on, thanks to the thousands of dollars it costs to pay for employees, storage, photography, insurance, shipping, and travel.

Paint by numbers: With so many factors, the art business can be more off-balance than a pair of Vincent van Gogh’s glasses. But, on average, the New York Times estimates that a small-to-midsize gallery could bring in about $295,000 in monthly revenue against $91,000 in costs.—BC

items.title: The art auction slowdown is over
items.summary: Peter Parks/Getty Images For a moment there, it seemed like nobody wanted to own precious paintings anymore. But after art sales at auctions worldwide declined between 2022 and 2025, sky-high gavel poundings this year have all but erased the market’s freefall. Sales at…
items.author: Molly Liebergall
items.contentHtml:
For a moment there, it seemed like nobody wanted to own precious paintings anymore. But after art sales at auctions worldwide declined between 2022 and 2025, sky-high gavel poundings this year have all but erased the market’s freefall.

Sales at Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips hit $6.8 billion in the first half of the year, a 70% year-over-year increase that was in part propelled by demand for famous 20th-century works:

  • The global auction market hasn’t performed this well since the first half of 2022, when it netted $7.1 billion, according to Bank of America.
  • Hot commodities this year included a Jackson Pollock bought for $181.2 million—making it the fourth most expensive artwork ever sold at public auction—and a Mark Rothko that went for $98.4 million.
  • Christie’s noted that fine art remains its most important category, but auction houses’ overall sales were also buoyed by collectibles—an entry-point category for many younger bidders that includes trading cards, watches, and even dinosaur fossils.

Art Basel tea leaves: The median disclosed sale price at Switzerland’s famous art fair nearly tripled to $287,500 this year, suggesting a broad pickup in spending that extends beyond the wealthiest collectors, per Maddox Gallery.

This month brings another doozy of an auction

If you have several million dollars to spare, mark your calendar for Nov. 18 in New York. That’s when Sotheby’s will auction off a famous 12-painting collection that’s been likened to “a small museum” with “almost mythical status in the art world.” All in, the artwork is expected to net $450+ million.

Desirable No. 1: “Châtaigniers en fleurs,” a rare Van Gogh, is projected to sell for at least $180 million, which would shatter the artist’s previous public auction record of $117 million in 2022.

But…despite the art world’s auction momentum, galleries are struggling, a former Art Basel global director wrote earlier this year. One reason may be that collectors are leaning away from emerging artists and embracing established, historical names—aka an auction house’s bread and butter.—ML

items.title: The Wound of Love
items.summary: Welcome to The Unsolicited Advice Reading Group. This month we are reading Anne Carson’s book Eros The Bittersweet . Our schedule will be as follows: Saturday 7th November - Up to “Alphabetic Edge” Saturday 14th November - Up to “Folded Meanings” Saturday 21st November - Up to…
items.author: Joseph Folley
items.contentHtml:
Welcome to The Unsolicited Advice Reading Group. This month we are reading Anne Carson’s book Eros The Bittersweet. Our schedule will be as follows:

Saturday 7th November - Up to “Alphabetic Edge”

Saturday 14th November - Up to “Folded Meanings”

Saturday 21st November - Up to “Cicadas”

Saturday 28th November - Up to the end

Saturday 5th December - Live call for paid subscribers (6PM UK time)

If you would like to join our live calls and get access to exclusive articles, consider becoming a paid subscriber :)

The primary organising idea of the first few chapters of Eros the Bittersweet is eros and romantic desire as a kind of felt lack, but a lack which the lover has a rather complex relationship with, and in some sense even desires to maintain.

The observation which sparks Carson’s thoughts here is the word that the ancient Greek lyric poet Sappho uses to describe her feelings of erotic love, glukupikron. Literally translated, this means “sweet-bitter”, though of course a much more natural English rendering of the word is “bittersweet”. This word obviously makes it into the title of Carson’s book, and also very much sets its tone. This is a book about the relationship between the “sweet” aspects of eros and the “bitter” ones. As Carson puts it:

“Love and hate converge within erotic desire. Why?”

The first initial answer that Carson gives to this question is in the idea of “lack”. As Carson points out, there is a long history of images which characterise love as a sense of loss or deprivation. Almost by definition, one cannot desire what is present. It would be a confusion of language to say that I “desire a copy of the first volume of The World as Will and Representation” when I can literally see my own copy on my coffee table as I am writing these words. Erotic desire, for Carson, is kept alive by this perpetual sense of dispossession. She quotes Simone Weil on this point:

“I want the person I love to love me. If he is, however, totally devoted to me he does not exist any longer and I cease to love him. And as long as he is not totally devoted to me he does not love me enough.”

It is tempting at this point to accuse Carson of not really studying eros itself, but rather some sort of unhealthy offshoot of it. Indeed, I think sometimes her chosen examples lend themselves to this reading, since she is often highlighting the bitter aspects of love as part of her thesis. However, I think this structure can be found even in healthy pairings. I have mentioned her before, but I quite enjoy the work of the relationships therapist Esther Perel. The testimony of experienced therapists is invaluable when studying something like love, because it strikes a compromise between breadth of study and depth of study. A broad quantitative study on love might capture many participants, but it abstracts away from the details of their particular experiences. On the other end of the spectrum, we can get a high level of detail if we reflect on our own relationships and our own experiences of love, but then we have a very small sample size, and so we totally lose generalisability. An experienced relationship therapist, while they necessarily study a self-selecting sample of “people who go to couples therapy” are still the best balance of these two factors in my view (the other source is great romantic literature, which demonstrates its applicability by the number of people who relate to it, and also provides some detail). I am sceptical of ever coming up with some grand theory of love with universal applicability and desirable depth, but that doesn’t mean we are resigned to total scepticism.

In Perel’s experience as a relationship therapist, she has found that the attraction in many of her couples is at its highest when two factors are kept in tension. On the one hand, there is emotional intimacy, such that the couple feel connected, but on the other hand there is a sense of separateness, whereby a sense of their independent existence as people is acknowledged. One example she points to is when someone sees their lover in a novel situation, which brings to light the fact that there are facets and crevices of this person that, despite their many years together, they still do not know about. This is reiterating in the context of a long-term relationship, precisely the observation that Carson makes about eros. By being made aware of undiscovered aspects to someone, the lover is reminded that, even in a long-term situation, there remains some distance between them, in which eros can be rekindled. This distance is part of Carson’s point - that eros thrives in the gap between the desire of the lover and the beloved themselves. She points out that much of Greek lyric poetry moves pretty swiftly from talking about the beloved to talking about the feeling created by the beloved’s absence. This is not just limited to poetry, we also see it in perhaps the most famous erotic image in Ancient philosophy: the myth of Aristophanes in Plato’s Symposium.

I’ve spoken about this before, but just to give a reminder, Aristophanes argued that humans were once eight-limbed beings that became powerful enough to rival the gods (at least collectively). To limit their power, they were cleaved in twain, separating them into two distinct four-limbed creatures instead. To hear Aristophanes tell it, we search for our “other half” because we really want to make ourselves whole again. I think the details of this image are unfortunate (for instance, I think it perpetuates the myth that there is one distinct, pre-existing person out there for everyone, and thus it places less emphasis on how we create love with our actions) but it represents one thing very well - the sense of incompleteness that is created by erotic desire and by love. The beloved is experienced as something desired, but not as one might desire a new book - as something to be added to the sum total of what someone already has, but instead as one who has fallen sick might desire health - as if something has been positively taken from them. In this case, what has been taken is the feeling of wholeness experienced before the sudden intense desire for the beloved. Aristophanes represents this lack or loss as a wound, and I like that as an image. There is something phenomenologically apt about it. Carson even presents Sappho as, at points in her poetry, fantasising about not being affected by her beloved, and so reclaiming this chunk that has been bitten out of her and restoring her sense of wholeness. Though she never actually does this, because (and get ready to hear a lot of phrases like this) while eros is bitter, it is also sweet.

The precise characterisation of this lack changes as the chapters go on. In the first few chapters, Carson seems to dwell on the strength of the desire and how it unsettles the lover, dominating their mind and inflicting them with this sense of loss, but in later chapters it is presented as a change which occurs in the self. As she puts it:

“As in the Greek poets, its pain arises at that edge where the self is adulterated and bitter verges alarmingly on sweet. Eros’ ambivalence unfolds directly from this power to ‘mix up’ the self. The lover helplessly admits that it feels both good and bad to be mixed up, but is then driven back upon the question ‘Once I have been mixed up in this way, who am I?’ Desire changes the lover.”

Eros is partly a compulsion to blend with the other, and to that extent both the desire itself and its fulfilment are, on this analysis, threats to the pre-existent self. This can be reacted to in a number of ways. While the Greek lyric poets often found it threatening or otherwise unpleasant, Carson points to other literary characters (such as those from Virginia Woolf’s The Waves) who find it more curious, and do not appear to be unsettled by this new perforated self. In his book A Secular Age, Charles Taylor argues that for your average medieval religious believer, they did not see their selves as something separate from the world, but continuous with it, and subject to the influence of all kinds of spirits, like a less exaggerated version of in Homer, where feelings are often represented (if that is the right word) by a god or a spirit acting on a character. He calls this phenomenon “the porous self”. If we combine Carson and Taylor’s analyses, then the feeling of eros approximates this porous self, and thus is it any wonder that we consider love a highly spiritual experience? Similar to Durkheim’s idea of collective effervescence, whereby we have quasi-religious experiences in various social settings where we feel a sense of unity with others, eros becomes transcendent. Not in the sense of implying the existence of a higher power, but in the sense of reaching beyond our physical boundaries, and placing our sense of self beyond our own skin. As we said, this can also be experienced as a kind of threat. I quite often feel somewhat torn when I catch myself in situations of collective effervescence, such as during musical performances. On the one hand it feels quite magical, but on the other there is this sense that I am losing myself in the crowd, and that always makes me nervous. I think Carson’s observation about the sense of threat to the self found in eros also extends to situations like this.

Given that eros arises in the tension between the distance that exists between the lover and the beloved, as well as the desire to cross that distance, Carson argues that we employ various techniques to extend and amplify that gap between us and our beloved, even when the feeling is mutual. Some of the ancient rituals she describes are quite horrific (and of dubious consent) such as ritual abduction, but these are at the far end of a spectrum with more tame elements to it as well. To use more modern examples, we could place in this category things like “playing hard to get” (within reason), as well as the kind of mutual teasing that I often see in loving couples. Within Carson’s framework, these can be seen as attempts to create the kind of play-tension conducive to eros. I am reminded of the observations made by both Stendhal and Dorothy Tennov that love and limerence often reach their most intense forms precisely when hope of victory and risk of defeat hang in a delicate balance. This too seems to play with that tension between blending and separateness that Carson identifies or, as she puts it elsewhere, the connection between eros and questions of limit and transgression.

If we (as Carson does) conceive of eros as somewhat transgressive in nature, then the relationship between desire and distance become a little bit clearer. For Carson, what the lover appears to desire is not that the distance disappears, but that the distance is continually being overcome. There is something Nietzschean about this picture, and it reminds me of Reginster’s analysis of Nietzsche’s will to power, where it is interpreted as the overcoming of greater and greater resistances, without a proper end in sight. But of course, as Carson points out, this makes eros often a slightly self-defeating or paradoxical feeling. It both desires to overcome the distance between the lover and the beloved, but also to maintain it.

I actually think that the horrifying end-point of unlimited erotic transgression, where distance is never restored and the lover just keeps pushing, is found in the works of the Marquis de Sade (I can’t remember if Carson mentions this later on or if I am just projecting passages from Camus’ The Rebel onto her). I’ve been meaning to make a video about Sade’s philosophy for ages, because he is quite an important figure in intellectual history. Most people focus on the fact that his books are shocking and disgusting, and largely consist of the horrible violation of the innocent by the powerful for their own twisted gratification. But to be honest, the main reason I have struggled to engage with his work is because it is just so tiresome. After about two hundred pages, Sade has totally exhausted the narrative interest of transgression, and all he can do is endlessly repeat the same depictions of horrifying suffering over and over again until the reader becomes numb. It’s not just that it isn’t erotic, it’s not even disgusting anymore. The reader becomes so inured that there are no more limits to transgress, but the book keeps going, agonisingly racking your patience for hundreds more pages until you have to stop, not because you are nauseated but because you are bored of it. The interesting thing about Sade’s work is that it ceases to shock pretty quickly, because Sade does not recognise any limits. There is more interesting narrative tension in whether Madame Bovary will cheat on her husband than whether victim-number-whatever will be brutally abused and murdered, because while the first is a far lesser transgression, the second occurs in a story where all the limits are already crossed, and no longer seem to mean anything.

Obviously Sade is the most extreme example of transgression (or at least the most extreme one I have encountered), but in his example we can see the importance of limits to a sense of the erotic. Even apart from the repellant content, Sade’s works are antithetical to the erotic because they have no respect for boundaries or desire to maintain them. Compare that with the build up to Julien Sorel’s first love affair in The Red and The Black. There are chapters and chapters full of looks left for interpretation, snatches of conversation, questions of whether she shared Sorel’s feelings. The limits between them are transgressed eventually (though certainly not like in Sade) but it is in the tension created in those moments that the book is at its most eros-infused, and certainly when Julien’s feelings are most inflamed.

If we put the wound-framing and the observations on limits together, then we end up with a vivid phenomenological picture of Carson’s eros. It is a felt lack in the self that can only be healed by the transgression of the boundary between the self and the other, while never quite overcoming it completely. It is eros conceived of as a dynamic relation, rather than a mere feeling. I am not sure whether I agree with it completely, but there is definitely something in it. I would like to see this kind of framework developed and applied to cases of mutual love or long-term partnership. I think that Perel’s books go some of the way here, but I would be interested to see whether this accurately characterises eros across many contexts and many different people, or if this an analysis that is best suited to particular stages of love or particular psychological constitutions.

Either way, I am looking forward to continuing our read-through next week, where we will discuss the way Carson uses these observations about eros to discuss language and writing.

items.title: November’s Hidden Mythic Word. Six Clues. Can You Solve It?
items.summary: Back by popular demand! Last month we published our first collaboration with Etymon, the daily puzzle for those who love word histories, and over seventeen thousand of you played the October puzzle. So we've decided to start a regular monthly collaboration, and Etymon has…
items.author: Myth and Mystery
items.contentHtml:
Back by popular demand! Last month we published our first collaboration with Etymon, the daily puzzle for those who love word histories, and over seventeen thousand of you played the October puzzle. So we've decided to start a regular monthly collaboration, and Etymon has created this new puzzle for Myth and Mystery readers. Guess which mythic word is hiding behind the series of clues leading back to ancient Greece!

How to play

Etymon is a daily puzzle about the origins of English words. One word hidden behind six clues drawn from its etymological history.

Each of the clues narrows the field, moving from era and origin through linguistic path, literal meaning, cognates, historical or geographical context, and word length toward the answer.

Some puzzlers achieve Solved in 1. More reach the answer at Solved in 4 or Solved in 5. Some work through to Solved in 6.

You can guess after any clue. How many will you need?

When you are ready, the Answer Card button at the bottom of this post will reveal the puzzle’s hidden word, etymology, and modern use on Etymon’s Substack.

Once you’ve checked the Answer Card, come back here to share your Solved in N score in the comments, and/or restack the banner matching the clue you solved it on to share your result on Substack Notes. We’d love to know how you got on!

  1. Era and origin. The word was first recorded in Old English. It appears in King Alfred’s translation of Pope Gregory’s Pastoral Care, in a line about an animal that rolls into a ball when it is caught.

  1. Linguistic path. Middle English probably lost the last letter of the Old English word, and the spelling we use today appeared in the 15th century. Around 1385 Chaucer’s Legend of Good Women describes a jailer leaving a man’s weapon and ball of thread in a house.

  1. Literal meaning. Behind it lay an older Germanic word for a ball, from which the Old English word was probably built to mean a small ball. That Germanic word may trace to a Proto-Indo-European root, *gleu-, meaning ‘to gather into a mass’.

  1. Cognates. CLOD goes back to that same root, and CLOUD is related to CLOD. CLOD was an Old English word for ‘a lump of earth or clay’. CLOUD was an Old English word for ‘a mass of rock, a hill’, and by about 1300 came to name a mass of vapour in the sky.

  1. Historical or geographical context. In 1821 Byron’s play Sardanapalus applied the word to the thread of life that the Fates spin. And in 1886 Fergus Hume’s novel The Mystery of a Hansom Cab applied it to what a cabman told the detectives hunting a murderer.

  1. Word length. Four letters.

items.title: Tesla is pulling the plug on the Cybertruck
items.summary: Morning Brew Inc. The most common reason for someone to start posting pictures from the highway will soon be no more. Tesla will stop producing the Cybertruck at its Texas Gigafactory by mid-2027, Elon Musk said yesterday. Musk said the move is meant to make room for the…
items.author: Sam Klebanov
items.contentHtml:
The most common reason for someone to start posting pictures from the highway will soon be no more. Tesla will stop producing the Cybertruck at its Texas Gigafactory by mid-2027, Elon Musk said yesterday.

Musk said the move is meant to make room for the company’s autonomous Cybercab. The decision to nix what was once Tesla’s most hyped vehicle comes after the Cybertruck became a commercial flop, hitting just 10% of its sales goal.

Shattered window dreams

At the Cybertruck’s 2019 unveiling—when Tesla’s design chief broke its supposedly bulletproof window—Musk billed the futuristic pickup truck as Tesla’s “best product ever.”

Tesla bet the Blade Runner-inspired stainless steel design, planned $40,000 price tag, and a version with a 500-mile charging range would make it the first EV to dominate the lucrative pickup market. But like a brutalist municipal building, the head-turning creation looked more promising in the blueprint:

  • After Covid delayed its initial release, the pickup’s late-2023 arrival in showrooms was met with lukewarm demand.
  • It didn’t help that the Cybertruck was plagued by tech issues that led to several recalls, ended up costing $60,000, and never had a range that surpassed 325 miles.

Few takers: While Musk predicted yearly sales would reach 250,000 vehicles, just under 73,000 have been sold in total so far, per data from Motor Intelligence. The vehicle continues to have a cult following among Musk fans. But sales dropped sharply after he vocally backed President Trump, and it turned into a polarizing symbol amid the Tesla CEO’s controversial effort to downsize the government. US sales dropped to 20,237 in 2025 from 38,965 in 2024—and are down a further 28% this year.

Looking ahead: After the Cybertruck rides into the sunset, Tesla will have just two human-driven models in production, the Model 3 and the Model Y (its Roadster airborne sports car isn’t scheduled to start production until 2028). The company is going full throttle with plans for a nationwide rollout of its two-seater autonomous Cybercabs, which are already ferrying passengers in Austin.—SK

items.author: Dave Lozo
items.contentHtml:
An Italian chef working in Australia claimed he was wrongly fired from his job for refusing to put pineapple on pizza, telling the country’s Fair Work Commission the dish is an “insult to his culture.”

The commission dismissed Davide Tamburella’s claim on the grounds that he filed it too late, not that he was wrong. The La Costa restaurant, located in Queensland, has since closed. The state produces 100% of the country’s commercial pineapples and is home to a 52-foot-tall pineapple called The Big Pineapple (makes sense).

But, just like a Chicago pizza, this goes deeper:

  • Tamburella’s bosses cited his foul language and communication style as reasons for his firing in the ruling, which also included a claim that he broke his hand punching a metal railing.
  • This was allegedly the third time in four years that he refused to put pineapple on pizza.

Most surveys show that Americans are split on the tropical fruit topping, but one poll in 2023 found that 72% of Australians love it.

In the end, Tamburella got a new job at another Italian restaurant in Brisbane that does not have pineapple pizza on the menu.—DL

items.title: November 6, 2026
items.summary: November 6, 2026 Reader 📏 NEW! Text Width on Phones — The Text width option in the Appearance sheet only showed up on tablets, so on a phone the text always ran close to the edges of the screen, which makes selecting near the edge fiddly. Artem brought the setting to phones in…
items.contentHtml:
November 6, 2026

Reader

  • 📏 NEW! Text Width on Phones — The Text width option in the Appearance sheet only showed up on tablets, so on a phone the text always ran close to the edges of the screen, which makes selecting near the edge fiddly. Artem brought the setting to phones in the Reader app and the Readwise Books app, so you can pick wider margins anywhere you read.
  • 🗂️ Improved iPhone Duo Navigation — On the iPhone Duo, the Reader app kept the bottom tab bar even on the closed outer screen, where navigation belongs on a vertical rail. Cam turned on the side rail for everyone so it shows on the closed Duo and when the Duo is open in landscape. Every other phone keeps the tab bar.
  • 🔄 Improved Cross-Device Reading — If you had a document open on one device, read further on another, then came back, the first device stayed where it was, with no way to jump ahead short of closing and reopening the document. Thanks to Johannes, the Reader app and the Readwise Books app now show the return-to-reading button as soon as your newer position syncs, and tapping it takes you to where you left off.
  • 🧠 Improved BYOK Models — If you bring your own OpenAI key to Ghostreader in Reader, you can now pick GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, and GPT-6.1 Terra. Ibai added them to the model list, and chat and skills work with all three.
  • 🔉 Improved Lifelike Voice Volume — The Lifelike voices in Reader's text-to-speech could play quietly, and the volume could jump from one paragraph to the next. Artem now evens out the loudness of every paragraph, so Lifelike voices play at a steady level that matches the other voices.
  • ⚡ Improved Sync for Large Libraries — When the Reader app fully synced a library of more than 5,000 documents, it fetched the first batch twice and threw one copy away. Tristan cut the extra fetch, so big libraries should finish their first sync noticeably sooner.
  • ✖️ Fixed Close Buttons — On iOS, tapping the X on the Continue bar at the bottom of the Reader app opened the document instead of closing the bar. The X in the expanded text-to-speech player and on the Daily Digest card on Home did the same. Tristan and Artem fixed all three, so each X just closes what it's on.
  • 👀 Fixed Feed Swipe View — Flicking quickly through the feed's swipe view in the Reader app on iOS didn't always mark the articles you passed as seen, so they came back the next time you opened the feed. Tristan made every article you swipe past count as seen.
  • 🎬 Fixed YouTube Next Video — Swiping from one YouTube video to the next in the Reader app on iOS played the new video's sound behind a black screen. Johannes fixed the player, so the next video shows up along with its audio.
  • 🖋️ Fixed Italic Text — In the Reader app, italic text set in Public Sans displayed upright, so emphasis and italic passages in EPUBs looked like the rest of the text. Johannes pointed the font at its real italic file, so italics display as italics again.
  • 🖍️ Fixed Highlight Resizing on iOS — Dragging the handles to resize a highlight in the Reader app on iOS turned the selection black, hiding the text you were trying to select. Adam fixed the selection color, so you can see what you're highlighting as you adjust it.
  • ⬅️ Fixed Android Back Gestures — On Android 16, once you backed out of the Reader app to your home screen, every later back gesture skipped Reader's own navigation and sent you home, even from inside an article. Back also wouldn't close the share sheet, which saved the page again each time you pressed it. Johannes fixed both, so back behaves the way you'd expect.
  • 📄 Fixed Page Turns While Selecting — Pressing a volume button to turn the page in the Reader app on Android while selecting text turned the page anyway, stretching the selection across both pages until the highlight was too long to save. Artem made the page wait until you finish selecting.
  • 🏷️ Fixed Tags and Notes on Android — Switching between the Note and Tags tabs on a highlight in the Reader app on Android closed the keyboard every time, and the sheet jumped as it did. Artem kept both fields ready, so you can switch tabs and keep typing.
  • 👉 Improved iPad Toolbar Swipes — Swiping the modern toolbar in the Reader app on an iPad in landscape took a drag across nearly the whole screen. Johannes shortened the distance, so a landscape swipe feels the same as one in portrait.
  • 💬 Fixed Ghostreader Follow-Ups — In the Ghostreader sidebar on Reader web, selecting a new passage and asking about it later in a long chat could get you an answer about a passage from earlier in the conversation. Tristan now keeps each question's selected passage with it, so Ghostreader answers about the text you just picked.
  • 🀄 Fixed Summaries for Chinese Documents — Ghostreader's Summarize prompt in Reader could reply that no article text was provided for long Chinese, Japanese, or Korean documents. Tristan fixed how Reader picks the key sentences from those documents, so long CJK articles get a real summary.
  • ⌨️ Fixed Numpad Page Keys — With NumLock off, pressing PgDn on the number pad in Reader on web jumped to your Feed instead of paging down, because it triggered the 3 shortcut. Tristan made the numpad's PgUp, PgDn, Home, and End keys page through the document like the regular keys.
  • 🔌 Improved Reader API for Books — Setting reading_progress through the Reader API worked for articles but not for EPUBs, which are the documents most people track progress on. Tristan added EPUB support, and Reader on web now opens the book in the right chapter for the progress you set.
  • 📻 Fixed RSS Articles with Audio — Substack articles with a voiceover showed up as podcasts in Reader, and articles from a few news sites that attach a narration file lost their text entirely. Krzys now labels those feed items as articles, so you get the full text in your feed.
  • 🛜 Parsing Updates — Krzys improved how Reader handles documents from nytimes.com, substack.com, github.com, newyorker.com, wikipedia.org, mp.weixin.qq.com, note.com, every.to, claude.dev, emcrit.org, and seangoedecke.com.

Highlights

  • 📲 NEW! CrossPoint Sync — If you read on a CrossPoint, CrossInk, or KOReader e-reader, you'll now find CrossPoint on the Readwise Highlights import page. Its Connect button takes you to CrossPoint Sync, where you link your Readwise account, and your highlights flow into Readwise from there. Thanks to Ibai for adding the tile.
  • 📑 Improved Book Pages on Web — Book pages in Readwise Highlights on the web were a single centered column, and the table of contents only appeared on very wide screens as a floating card. Ibai rebuilt them into two columns: the cover, details, and a full table of contents stay put on the left while your highlights scroll on the right, and the section you're in is marked. Smaller windows get the same layout as the app's book page.
  • 🔠 Improved Fonts in Daily Review — The Readwise Highlights app switched to Plus Jakarta Sans a while back, but Daily Review, stats, book pages, and Ghostreader chat inside the app still used older fonts, so a sheet over a review card didn't match the card under it. Ibai moved those screens to Plus Jakarta Sans too, which also brings Vietnamese letters to Daily Review.
  • 🔁 Fixed Repeating Mastery Cards — In Readwise Highlights, some mastery cards kept coming back in Daily Review however you graded them, and a few couldn't be graded at all. Skipping a few days of reviews could also show the same card once for every day you missed. Ibai fixed both, so a mastery card shows up once and moves on when you grade it.
  • 🎙️ Fixed Silent Audio Reviews — An audio Daily Review in Readwise Highlights could play its intro and then go quiet for a minute or more while the script behind it got stuck. Tristan made the review notice a stuck script and retry within a second or two, so the audio should keep going after the intro.
  • 🚫 Fixed Never Highlights in Widgets — Highlights you'd marked Never in Daily Review still turned up in the Readwise Highlights home screen widget. Johannes keeps them out of the widget now, and out of the highlights used for themed review and chat suggestions. Choosing Soon, Later, or Someday on a highlight brings it back.
  • 📘 Fixed Supplemental Books — Syncing Goodreads to Readwise Highlights could add supplemental highlights for books you'd already highlighted yourself through clippings or a manual import, so your own books showed up twice. Ibai now matches those books by title, so new supplementals skip books you already have.
  • 🕒 Fixed Kindle Sync Date — The Kindle "Last synced" date on the Readwise Highlights import page could be wrong in both directions: failed attempts moved it forward, and syncs you started yourself didn't count. Ibai made it show your last sync that actually finished.
  • 📦 Improved CSV Exports — Exporting a very large Readwise Highlights library to CSV could run for many minutes, because each batch reread every remaining highlight. Piotr now reads highlights one batch of books at a time, so big exports should finish much faster.
  • 📅 Fixed Renewal Reminder Dates — The email reminding you that an annual Readwise plan is about to renew could show the day after the real renewal date if you renew in the evening in the US, so you could miss the window to cancel. Tristan now shows the date in your own time zone.

Books

  • 🔗 NEW! Goodreads Cross-Posting — If you connect Goodreads to Readwise Books, you can now have Books post to your Goodreads account for you. Open Settings > Integrations > Goodreads (or Goodreads in your Library) and choose what to cross-post: shelf changes, ratings and reviews, and reading progress from your sessions. Each one has its own toggle and starts off, so if you write your reviews on Goodreads you can leave that one off and still sync your shelves. When you finish a book, Books also sends your start and finish dates. Thanks to Mati for building this integration.
  • ⚙️ NEW! Kindle and Goodreads Screens — Your Kindle and Goodreads connections in Readwise Books each have their own screen now, under Settings > Integrations or from your Library. From there you can refresh, disconnect Goodreads while keeping everything you imported, or delete an integration and its data. Refreshing runs in a small status pill, so you can keep using the app instead of waiting on a full-screen import. The Kindle screen is also where you'll find the Continuous scroll option for Kindle books. Thanks again to Mati.
  • 📤 NEW! EPUB Uploads in the Books API — Thanks to Piotr, developers and AI agents can now add EPUBs to Readwise Books through the Books API and the Readwise MCP server, not only through the app. Upload one book or a batch and pick the shelf they land on. The readwise.io/books/upload page can now pick a shelf too.
  • 🤖 Improved Books API and MCP — The Readwise Books app never pointed you to its API or MCP server, and listing a big library through MCP could return more text than an AI assistant could take in. Piotr added a Developers (API/MCP) row under Settings > Connections in the app. He also trimmed the publisher summary out of book lists by default and added small cover images. Audiobook length can now be set through the API too, so audiobook sessions logged that way show your progress.
  • 📖 Improved Kindle Books on iPad — Kindle books in Readwise Books showed one wide column on an iPad in landscape, while the same book in Safari showed two. Mati taught the app to lay out two columns in landscape on iPad, so it reads like an open book.
  • 🔘 Improved Kindle Books on Boox Devices — Reading Kindle books in Readwise Books on Boox devices had a few rough spots. The page buttons did nothing, the loading screen could pop up mid-read and move you back a few lines, and on Android the top bar stayed on screen over the first line of text. Mati fixed all three, so the page buttons turn pages and the reader stays out of the way.
  • 🎧 Fixed Audiobooks During Calls — When a call came in during an audiobook in Readwise Books, Android kept playing the book under the ringtone and counted it as listening time, and iPhone paused it but never started it again. Johannes made audiobooks pause for calls and similar interruptions and pick back up when they end.
  • 🎟️ Improved Invite Codes — A Readwise Books invite code stopped working after five friends used it, and the next friend saw "Invite code not found". Tristan now adds five more invites when a code fills up and sends the inviter a thank-you, so your link keeps working. Inviters also get the "joined Readwise Books" notification with their friend's real handle.
  • 🗨️ Improved Book Page Reviews — The Reviews tab on a book page in Readwise Books repeated the whole book card, cover and blurb included, under every single review. Tristan turned each review into a compact card with the reviewer, stars, and date, and reviews from people you follow come first.
  • 🕰️ Fixed Last Session Popup — The Last session recap in Readwise Books popped up nearly every time you opened a book, and its X sometimes didn't close it. Artem added a time limit, so it shows at most once every six hours per book, and Mati made the X always close it.
  • 📍 Fixed Reopening After Listening — After you listened to a book with text-to-speech in Readwise Books and then kept reading, reopening the book could take you back to where the audio had been instead of where you stopped reading. Artem cleared the old listening spot, so books reopen at your latest position.
  • 🏃 Fixed Missing Reading Sessions — Some real reading sessions in Readwise Books never showed up in the feed, like ones where you jumped back to an earlier chapter or saved your place back where you started. The reading recap could also show lower totals than Home for the same week. Tristan and Johannes fixed both, so your sessions appear in the feed and your recap matches Home.
  • 🏆 Improved Readerboard History — Past weeks on the Readwise Books Readerboard could change after the week was over when a session synced late or was deleted, and the podium used a different week than the board. Piotr now locks each week's board at midnight Pacific when the week ends, and the podium follows the same week.
  • 🛒 Fixed Kindle Shelf — A book you'd bought on Kindle after removing an earlier copy from Readwise Books could be left off your shelf, so the import said 25 books while your library showed 24. Tristan now puts new purchases on the shelf. Mati also added a note to the Kindle shelf's book sheet explaining that you need to move the book into your Library to read it.
  • 🔀 Fixed Goodreads Connections — Connecting Goodreads in Readwise Books could sit on "Connecting to Goodreads…" indefinitely when the page hit a network error or an unexpected Goodreads screen, and imports could time out on their first page. Mati added a timeout and a fallback, so you either see Goodreads' sign-in page or a clear error, and a stalled import reloads and carries on.
  • 🩹 Fixed Books That Wouldn't Open — Some ebooks bought from the Readwise Books store showed their cover and a spinner forever, because one of their stylesheets had a character our parser choked on. Tristan made the parser tolerate it, so those books open normally.
  • 📕 Fixed Books Skipping the Introduction — Some ebooks you uploaded to Readwise Books and Reader opened at Chapter 1 and skipped the Introduction and other front matter before it. Samuel fixed how the reader picks the starting page, so books open where they actually begin.
  • 🖼️ Improved EPUB Images — Small illustrations in some EPUBs rendered far too large in Readwise Books and Reader, and pages could shift as images loaded in. Artem now sizes each image from the book's own layout before it arrives and keeps it within the page, so pictures appear at the size the publisher intended.
  • 📐 Fixed Foldable Margins — Opening a book in Readwise Books or the Reader app on the folded outer screen of an Android foldable and then unfolding it kept the narrow phone margins, so the text ran nearly edge to edge on the big screen. Cam made the margins follow the screen you're using.
  • 🔍 Fixed Match to Bookshop on Android — Tapping a result in Match to Bookshop in Readwise Books on Android did nothing, so you couldn't link a book to its store edition. Tristan fixed the sheet, so picking a result works on Android the way it does on iPhone.
  • 🆓 Fixed Free Ebook Checkout — Trying to buy a free ebook in the Readwise Books store with Buy Now ended in an error. Tristan fixed the free checkout path, so $0 books go straight to your library.
  • 🙋 Improved Mentions and Bios — Typing someone's exact handle in a Readwise Books comment didn't put them first in the suggestions, and your own handle never appeared. A profile bio wrapped in quotation marks also showed only a closing quote. Tristan fixed both, so mentions find the right person and quoted bios display in full.

items.author: Tim Ferriss
items.contentHtml:
Please enjoy this transcript of a special episode of The Tim Ferriss Show, featuring not a guest but a number. As this is episode #888, I couldn’t resist going down a rabbit hole about the number eight and what it can tell us about luck, language, money, and fate. Join me for a nerdy tour of China, Japan, and Korea, including a million-dollar license plate, disappearing hotel floors, a casino room designed around one gambler’s birthday, and the lucky number hiding in Toyota’s name. This is my excuse to dust off some of my East Asian Studies background and indulge a few wonderfully weird interests.

Books, people, tools, and resources mentioned in the interview

Legal conditions/copyright information

Listen onApple Podcasts
Listen onOvercast
Lucky #888 — My Tour of Designing Luck in China, Japan, and Korea

Additional podcast platforms

Listen to this episode on Apple Podcasts, , Overcast, Podcast Addict, Pocket Casts, Castbox, YouTube Music, Amazon Music, Audible, or on your favorite podcast platform.

Transcripts may contain a few typos. With many episodes lasting 2+ hours, it can be difficult to catch minor errors.

Tim Ferriss: All righty. Hello, boys and girls, ladies and germs. This is Tim Ferriss. Welcome to another episode of The Tim Ferriss Show. This episode is a special one. It is number 888. That’s triple eight. We’re going to talk about it. This is going to be a rabbit hole of epic proportions, and it’s going to get nerdy.

It’s going to get very bizarre, and that’s the point of the show is I can kind of do whatever I want to do. So I wanted to do something special for 888. I thought about doing some live casting of the I Ching, the oldest of the Chinese classics. It’s a long story. Maybe we’ll come back to that. But let’s talk about luck. If you know anything about the Chinese ideas around luck, there’s one number that stands out. And I couldn’t resist.

So we’re going to talk about a very expensive phone number, disappearing hotel floors, a casino room designed around one person’s birthday, a car company whose name was chosen, or I should say changed, partly for good fortune, and it spans across East Asia. We’re going to dig in. Underneath all of it is one question. How do you design luck?

Can you build it into a skyscraper, a brand name, a license plate? Well, a lot of people would seem to think so. And what happens when a casino and the customer both want the room to make the money? Well, let’s dig in. So it starts with a sound. In Mandarin, the sound is ba, that is eight, the number eight. And I’ll say right up front that of the languages we’re going to touch upon, my strongest is going to be Japanese, then Mandarin, then Korean, which is going to be very weak. I studied it for one year in college, like 30 plus years ago. And then my Cantonese is non-existent. So basically ignore everything I say about Cantonese. In theory, it’ll make sense, but my pronunciation is going to suck.

But back to Mandarin. So eight is ba. Now the word fa shows up all over the place. And you’ll find it in, for instance, a common New Year’s greeting, which is gōngxǐ fācái. Gōngxǐ fācái is like, congratulations, may you prosper. It’s the fā is like to emerge or come out. So departure is like chūfā. And then the cái, the second tone cái, gōngxǐ fācái is riches, wealth, prosperity, all that good stuff. So in a sense, the fācái, to find riches, prosperity, to have all this emerge into your life, gets represented by the fa, which then corresponds to [bā?].

So there you have it. That’s where eight becomes lucky. It’s the resemblance. Now in Cantonese, the match is even closer. I’m not going to try to say it because Cantonese is hard AF, even if you speak Mandarin. But you will recognize some similarities because the writing system is the same. And also Japan and Korea borrowed their writing systems at one point in time from China, and we can dig into a lot of the later developments. But you’ll hear, for instance: Gōngxǐ fācái in Mandarin is going to be something like [Cantonese greeting attempt, repeated; uncertain], something like that in Cantonese. It’s the same characters. So that’s the sound connection and why 8 is such a popular prosperity symbol in Chinese-speaking communities.

And this goes back a long, long ways. However, it was supercharged, it seems, in the 1980s. And especially in Hong Kong, and then it kind of expanded from there. And Gordon Gekko, man, greed is good. Let’s get after the money. And I always have to laugh because some folks who are reading these texts or translated, usually mistranslated texts from, Lao Tzu or whoever it might be, talk about, oh, the East, you know, if you could only look at the contrast outside of the materialist West.

And I’m like, you know, if you squint a little bit and look at some actual proper translations or the original text, man, everybody loves money. And that certainly includes China. So eight great news, eight, eight, eight, three eights, three doses of good fortune. That’s linguistic compound interest. They love it. Now, look, not everyone believes this.

Not everyone believes it equally. But if a customer prefers it, well, guess what? Interesting things happen to prices. So as an example, in 2003, Sichuan Airlines paid 2.33 million yuan, about 280,000 US at the time, for the phone number 8888-8888. So that’s eight eights for a customer hotline.

This is an extraordinary amount of money to spend before anyone has even said your call is important to us. But look, they explain it: the number is easy to remember, and it would make customers happy. Why? Because, well, [eights are?] good luck, like we already talked about. And for those language nerds out there, Sichuan, you might run into this. In, say, the U.S., there are Chinese restaurants that specialize in this particular type of cuisine. Some think of it as spicy. Sichuan means literally four rivers. Sì, yī, èr, sān, sì, Sìchuān. It’s actually an abbreviation related to administrative districts, but that gets to sound too bureaucratic, so let’s just stick with four rivers. Sichuan. In any case, this is the perfect intersection of superstition and marketing, right? Buying a number like this. Now, there are two benefits I should add, by the way, because not only do you get the benefit of whatever the eights mean to the customer, but you also get possibly the benefit of the PR halo and amplification around you buying the number.

So I don’t automatically assume that it was a bad decision, but who knows? My last conversation with Sichuan Airlines was a while ago. So anyway, license plates. In February 2025, the registration mark 8-8 sold at a Hong Kong government auction for 11.4 million Hong Kong dollars. That’s roughly 1.5 million US. Then we get to the calendar.

All right, Beijing Olympics. When are we going to have the opening ceremony? Well, of course, the opening ceremony should start at 8 p.m. on August 8th, 2008. That’s a lot of eights, right, on a global stage. Just so happens, on that same date, Beijing registered 15,646 marriages. So there you have it.

Next we have taking this number, this abstraction. I mean, we could get into where math lives, but that’s a whole separate convo. Maybe we should bring in Michael Levin. In any case, let’s talk about eights being put into the physical world. All right. The part that really gets interesting is when you stop buying lucky numbers and start building them.

For instance, Shanghai’s Jin Mao Tower, 88 stories. This is going to be very common around Asia. The architect, Adrian Smith, had said that the client wanted that number because eight was auspicious and it doesn’t stop at floor count. The building also has an octagonal core and eight main superframe columns. So eight is doing double duty. You got the cultural symbolism and then the actual structural work.

It shows up in ordinary apartments as well. Economists studied apartment sales in Chengdu from 2004 to 2006. Apartments on floors ending in eight resold at a premium of about 7%. In the new apartment market, where pricing was uniform, those floors didn’t cost more, but they sold about a week faster instead. And not shockingly, buyers with more eights in their phone numbers were more likely to buy the lucky floors.

Yeah, well, if you like eights, you like eights. And now we can also look at the flip side, though. If eight is lucky, right, that’s the whole premise. Well, it’s not really the premise. It is the topic we’re exploring in this episode. What is the flip side? The flip side is four. So now it’s not because half of eight is four, although we could talk about that. But we’re going to turn towards something a little more morbid, and that is death, because in Mandarin, four is si, and to die is si.

That is a fourth tone and a third tone, respectively. So you have like si, si, si, si. Those are four different things. So four is, as we covered already, si, chuan, si, si. To die is si. Same consonant, same vowel, different tone. This is where heads explode if you’re doing Chinese 101.

Way back in the day before Chinese was super cool. This is in, God, 1996, I guess. And we started with a class of something like 32 students. And within two weeks, we were down to like 12 or 14. People’s heads just exploded. And it will make your throat sore. It doesn’t matter how good you are at memorizing.

If you haven’t developed the musculature to make some of these sounds and tones and stuff, you just can’t do it. So it is actually like weight training in a sense. But let’s talk about four. Well, in the U.S., you might not see a floor 13. Well, guess what? In East Asia, all over the place, you will frequently not see floor numbers with a four.

That’s also true in places like Vietnam, by the way. But let’s talk about casinos. Where designing a place that feels lucky is practically its own art form. It isn’t practically, it is its own art form. This is a very, very important aspect of certain casino architectural plans. And in 2004, Time reported that Sands Macao replaced the slot machines, classic winning 777 with 888.

Then you have feng shui masters. Why not bring in a feng shui master? The design process can get very elaborate. In a 2005 interview, Las Vegas Sands executive William Weidner, sorry for mispronouncing that, I’m not sure of how that’s Americanized, Weidner described designers making 3D views of their plans, putting them on DVDs and flying them to a feng shui master in Kowloon, Hong Kong.

High-tech architecture software followed by an international trip to get the energy reviewed. So feng shui, another language sidebar. Feng shui, a lot of people have heard this. Feng shui, feng shui, that’s a one tone and a third tone, if you’re interested. That literally means wind, water. Feng shui, feng shui. So if some of you are wondering where the word typhoon comes from, pretty interesting.

So in Chinese you would say [táifēng, repeated; pronunciation uncertain]. And then there is false cognates. That’s a whole thing. So it turns out that, in fact, we didn’t get it directly from Chinese. There was this convergence of people calling typhoons the exact same thing. Basically, you had Greek-informed languages, then Arabic and the Chinese all somehow mysteriously converged on the same label for the same thing.

So it became this international global expression used by those involved with the maritime arts. But I digress. Feng shui literally means wind water.
